folders.name: Adobe’s media cache
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Adobe Media Cache Files on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Yes.** The media cache is audio and video that Premiere, After Effects and Media Encoder processed so previews play smoothly, and Adobe says deleted cache files are recreated automatically when your media needs them.
summary: **Yes.** The media cache is audio and video that Premiere, After Effects and Media Encoder processed so previews play smoothly, and Adobe says deleted cache files are recreated automatically when your media needs them. Projects and footage aren’t in it.
**What it costs you:** time. The next open of a project is slower while files rebuild, which Adobe says to allow for on big projects.
**Does it come back?** Yes, for any project you open again. Cache made for footage you’ve since deleted never comes back, which is why clearing it pays.
folders.comes_back: Yes, for any project you open again. Cache made for footage you’ve since deleted never comes back, which is why clearing it pays.
folders.what: When you import some video and audio formats, Adobe’s video apps prepare versions they can read quickly: audio is conformed to `.cfa` files, MPEG video is indexed to `.mpgindex` files, and waveform peaks are saved as `.pek` files. A database keeps track of them all, and Premiere, After Effects and Media Encoder share it, so each app can reuse the others’ work.
folders.how_to_clear:
### From Premiere

1. To clear everything, choose **File › Close All Projects** first.
2. Open **Premiere › Settings › Media Cache**.
3. Click **Delete** next to **Remove Media Cache Files**.
4. Choose **Delete unused media cache files** (files made for media that can no longer be found) or **Delete all media cache files from the system**, then click **OK**.

Adobe adds that to remove all of them, restart Premiere and choose that option before opening any project.

### By hand

Adobe’s other method: quit Premiere, and After Effects and Media Encoder too since they share the cache, then delete the files in the Common folder above and empty the Trash. In Terminal:

```
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Adobe/Common/Media\ Cache\ Files/*
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Adobe/Common/Media\ Cache/*
```

### Let Premiere clean up

In the same Media Cache settings, choose **Automatically delete cache files older than** (90 days by default) or **Automatically delete oldest cache files when cache exceeds** (10% of the drive by default). After a restart, Premiere checks 10 minutes after launch, then weekly.
clear_commands:
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Adobe/Common/Media\ Cache\ Files/*
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Adobe/Common/Media\ Cache/*

folders.name: After Effects’ disk cache
folders.question: Is it safe to clear After Effects’ disk cache on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Yes.** The disk cache is frames After Effects already rendered, kept so previews don’t render them again.
summary: **Yes.** The disk cache is frames After Effects already rendered, kept so previews don’t render them again. Emptying it loses no work: compositions, projects and footage are untouched.
**What it costs you:** previews render again the next time you play them, so the first playback is slower.
**Does it come back?** Yes. The disk cache is on by default and fills again as you preview.
folders.comes_back: Yes. The disk cache is on by default and fills again as you preview.
folders.what: After Effects caches frames in memory while you work and, by default, on disk as well; blue bars in the Timeline panel mark frames cached to disk. The disk cache is persistent: frames stay after you close the project or quit, and the cache holds frames from every project you’ve opened, so another project that needs the same frames can reuse them.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. In After Effects, choose **Edit › Purge › All Memory & Disk Cache**, or click **Empty Disk Cache** in **Settings › Disk**.
2. To clear everything at once (disk cache, media cache and its database), use **Empty All Caches** in **Settings › Startup & Repair**.
3. For a version you no longer use, quit After Effects and move that version’s folder inside `~/Library/Caches/Adobe/After Effects` to the Trash, since emptying one version’s cache leaves the others.

### Stop it filling the drive

Lower **Maximum Disk Cache Size**, turn on **Enable Compressed Frames (Lossless)** to fit more frames in less space, or use **Choose Folder** to put the cache on a separate SSD. Turning off **Enable Disk Cache** stops it altogether, at the price of slower previews.

folders.name: Android emulators (AVDs)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Android emulators in ~/.android/avd?
folders.answer: **Yes, the ones you don’t use**, from Android Studio’s Device Manager.
summary: **Yes, the ones you don’t use**, from Android Studio’s Device Manager. Each emulator, or AVD, keeps its own disk images: the apps you installed, their data, an emulated SD card and saved snapshots.
**What it costs you:** everything on that virtual device. The Android system image it was made from stays in the SDK, so you can create a fresh emulator without downloading Android again.
**Does it come back?** Only as a new, empty device you create again. Its apps, sign-ins and snapshots don’t come back.
folders.comes_back: Only as a new, empty device you create again. Its apps, sign-ins and snapshots don’t come back.
folders.what: An Android Virtual Device (AVD) is an emulator profile: a hardware profile, a system image with the Android version, and a storage area of its own on your Mac. Google’s documentation describes that storage area as holding the device’s user data, such as installed apps and settings, and an emulated SD card.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Stop the emulator if it’s running: close its window, or choose Stop from its menu in Device Manager.
2. In Android Studio, open Device Manager: View › Tool Windows › Device Manager, or More Actions › Virtual Device Manager on the Welcome screen.
3. On the emulator you don’t need, click its menu and choose Delete.

To keep an emulator but empty it, choose Wipe Data from the same menu instead: installed apps and settings go, and the device stays in the list as if new.

Without Android Studio, the SDK’s command-line tools delete an AVD by name. Google now marks `avdmanager` as deprecated in favour of its new `android emulator` command, but it still does the job:

```
~/Library/Android/sdk/cmdline-tools/latest/bin/avdmanager delete avd -n <name>
```

folders.name: The Android SDK
folders.question: Is it safe to delete the Android SDK folder?
folders.answer: **No, not all of it** while you build Android apps: Android Studio, Gradle and the emulator all run from it.
summary: **No, not all of it** while you build Android apps: Android Studio, Gradle and the emulator all run from it. The packages you don’t use, such as old system images, platforms and build tools, are safe to remove in Android Studio’s SDK Manager.
**What it costs you:** a package you remove is gone until you install it again from the SDK Manager. Remove one a project still needs, and that project won’t build until it’s back.
**Does it come back?** Only by downloading it again. Delete the whole SDK and Android Studio can’t build or run apps until you reinstall it.
folders.comes_back: Only by downloading it again. Delete the whole SDK and Android Studio can’t build or run apps until you reinstall it.
folders.what: The Android SDK is the toolkit Android Studio uses to build, run and debug apps. Google’s SDK Manager downloads it as separate packages, each in its own folder:
folders.how_to_clear:
1. In Android Studio, choose Tools › SDK Manager.
2. In the SDK Platforms and SDK Tools tabs, clear the checkbox next to each package you don’t use any more: system images no emulator needs, platforms for API levels you no longer compile against, old build tools and NDK versions. A red X marks each pending removal.
3. Click Apply or OK, check the list, and confirm.

Without Android Studio, the SDK’s `sdkmanager` lists packages and uninstalls them by their SDK path. Google now marks it as deprecated in favour of its new `android sdk` command:

```
~/Library/Android/sdk/cmdline-tools/latest/bin/sdkmanager --list
~/Library/Android/sdk/cmdline-tools/latest/bin/sdkmanager --uninstall "system-images;android-<API level>;<variant>;<architecture>"
```

Either way, you see each package’s name and version before anything goes, which beats guessing from folder names in Finder.

folders.name: App data (Application Support)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Application Support on a Mac?
folders.answer: **No, not as a whole.**
summary: **No, not as a whole.** Application Support is where apps keep their own data: libraries, projects, chat history, downloaded content and settings too big for a preferences file. Deleting an app’s folder resets that app and can lose what you made in it.
**What you can remove:** the folders of apps you’ve already deleted. Moving an app to the Trash leaves its folder here, and once the app is gone for good, that folder is a leftover.
**Does it come back?** Only as an empty folder. An app creates a fresh one the next time it runs, but the old contents are gone.
folders.comes_back: Only as an empty folder. An app creates a fresh one the next time it runs, but the old contents are gone.
folders.what: Apple tells developers to keep an app’s data files here: the ones the app creates and manages for you, which can include your own data. Each app gets one folder, named after its app ID (`com.example.app`) or simply its name, such as `Slack`, `Google`, or `Code` for Visual Studio Code.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Look for folders whose app you no longer have. Match each name to an app: `com.spotify.client` is Spotify, and a plain name is usually the app’s own.
2. Check the app really is gone, from Applications and from `~/Applications`, and that nothing else from the same maker uses the folder. The `Google` folder, for example, holds data for Chrome and Google’s other apps.
3. If there might be something of yours inside, such as exports or saved games, copy it out first.
4. Move the folder to the Trash, and empty the Trash once you’re sure.

For apps you still use, don’t delete their folder to save space. Remove downloads, old projects or offline content in the app’s own settings instead. To remove an app along with what it keeps, use its uninstaller if it has one: Apple calls that the best way to remove an app and its related data.

folders.name: macOS downloads (AssetsV2)
folders.question: Can I delete /System/Library/AssetsV2 on a Mac?
folders.answer: **No.** AssetsV2 is where macOS keeps parts it downloads after it’s installed: Apple Intelligence and Siri models, voices, dictionaries, fonts, security data and software updates on their way in.
summary: **No.** AssetsV2 is where macOS keeps parts it downloads after it’s installed: Apple Intelligence and Siri models, voices, dictionaries, fonts, security data and software updates on their way in. System Integrity Protection guards it, and macOS fetches what it needs again.
**What frees space instead:** turning off features you don’t use, installing updates that are waiting, and clearing what’s yours elsewhere on the Mac.
**Does it come back?** Yes. macOS manages what’s in it, adding and replacing assets as features and updates need them.
folders.comes_back: Yes. macOS manages what’s in it, adding and replacing assets as features and updates need them.
folders.what: macOS doesn’t ship with all of its optional parts. It downloads them when a feature needs them, through a system called MobileAsset, and keeps each kind in a folder named `com_apple_MobileAsset_` followed by its type. On a recent Mac you’ll find, among many others:
folders.how_to_clear:
You can’t delete it while macOS is running: SIP blocks it, even with `sudo`. Getting around that means starting up from Recovery or turning SIP off, and neither is worth it, since macOS can download the files again.

1. **Turn off what you don’t use.** On macOS 15 and 26, turning off Apple Intelligence in System Settings › Apple Intelligence & Siri removes its models. macOS 27 has no single switch: [what does and doesn’t free space there](https://siftmac.com/guides/apple-intelligence-storage).
2. **Install waiting updates.** If Software Update says an update has downloaded, install it rather than hunting for its files.
3. **Free space where you’re in charge:** old [iPhone backups](https://siftmac.com/guides/iphone-backups-on-mac), [macOS installers](https://siftmac.com/safe-to-delete/macos-installers) and [app caches](https://siftmac.com/safe-to-delete/library-caches).

folders.name: Bun’s cache (~/.bun)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Bun’s install cache?
folders.answer: **Yes, the cache part.**
summary: **Yes, the cache part.** `~/.bun/install/cache` holds packages Bun downloaded, and `bun pm cache rm` empties it. The rest of `~/.bun` can be Bun itself and your global tools, so keep it.
**What it costs you:** the next `bun install` in each project downloads again. Projects set up with Bun’s global store also need that install before they run.
**Does it come back?** Yes, with every `bun install`.
folders.comes_back: Yes, with every `bun install`.
folders.what: Depending on how you installed Bun, `~/.bun` can hold the tool itself as well as its cache:
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Stop `bun install`, `bun dev` and anything else Bun is running.
2. In a project folder, see what would be deleted, then clear it.

```
bun pm cache rm --dry-run
bun pm cache rm
```

This deletes everything in the cache folder, the global store in `links/` included, and keeps the folder itself. Bun can’t remove a single package this way: `bun pm cache rm <package>` is an error. For one package with stale registry data, Bun’s docs suggest `bun add <pkg> --force` or `bun update <pkg>` instead of clearing.

One quirk: `bun pm cache rm` takes the folder from `BUN_INSTALL_CACHE_DIR`, `--cache-dir` or `BUN_INSTALL`, and ignores a cache folder named in `bunfig.toml`. If you moved the cache there, pass the same folder with `--cache-dir`.

Don’t delete `~/.bun` as a whole unless you mean to remove Bun: with the install script, that takes the `bun` command and your global tools with it.
clear_commands:

bun pm cache rm

folders.name: Cargo’s registry and git cache
folders.question: Is it safe to delete ~/.cargo/registry and ~/.cargo/git?
folders.answer: **Yes**, those two. They’re Cargo’s cache of crates and git dependencies, which Cargo extracts or downloads again.
summary: **Yes**, those two. They’re Cargo’s cache of crates and git dependencies, which Cargo extracts or downloads again. Don’t delete `~/.cargo` as a whole: with rustup, its `bin` folder holds `cargo` and `rustc` themselves.
**What it costs you:** the next build re-extracts or downloads the crates it needs, and needs the network for anything no longer cached.
**Does it come back?** Yes. Since Rust 1.88, Cargo also trims old cache files by itself.
folders.comes_back: Yes. Since Rust 1.88, Cargo also trims old cache files by itself.
folders.what: `~/.cargo` is Cargo’s home. The Cargo Book lists what’s in it, and only part of it is cache:
folders.how_to_clear:
Close editors running rust-analyzer and let builds finish, then remove the parts you want. In order, from cheapest to most costly to rebuild:

```
rm -rf ~/.cargo/registry/src/*
rm -rf ~/.cargo/git/checkouts/*
rm -rf ~/.cargo/registry/cache/*
rm -rf ~/.cargo/git/db/*
```

The first two only cost re-extracting and checking out again, with no download. The last two mean downloading crates and cloning git dependencies again. The Cargo Book also mentions a third-party tool, `cargo-cache`, that shows the size of each part and clears them selectively.

Never run `rm -rf ~/.cargo` to save space. If you installed Rust with rustup, that removes `cargo`, `rustc` and `rustup` along with every program you installed.

folders.name: Google Chrome’s cache
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Google Chrome’s cache on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Yes.** Chrome’s cache is parts of pages it saved so sites open faster.
summary: **Yes.** Chrome’s cache is parts of pages it saved so sites open faster. Deleting it doesn’t touch bookmarks, passwords, history or extensions, and with **Cached images and files** ticked on its own, you stay signed in to sites.
**What it costs you:** slower first visits while Chrome downloads those parts again.
**Does it come back?** Yes, as you browse. Chrome refills it by itself, so clearing it fixes problems more than it frees space for good.
folders.comes_back: Yes, as you browse. Chrome refills it by itself, so clearing it fixes problems more than it frees space for good.
folders.what: Google’s own description: Chrome remembers parts of pages to help them open faster during your next visit. In practice that means images, scripts, fonts and code Chrome has already compiled. None of it is personal data you’d miss.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. In Chrome, click **More** (the three dots at the top right) and choose **Delete browsing data**. Typing *Delete browsing data* in the address bar opens the same dialog.
2. Set the time range to **All time**.
3. Tick **Cached images and files**. Untick **Cookies and other site data** and **Browsing history** if you want to keep your sign-ins and history.
4. Click **Delete data**.

The dialog works on the profile you’re in, so repeat it in each profile you use. Google notes that data you delete while signed in to Chrome is also removed from your other devices and your Google Account, one more reason to tick only the cache.

Leave `~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome` alone. Deleting it resets Chrome and loses everything that isn’t synced to your Google Account.

folders.name: Chrome’s on-device AI model
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Chrome’s OptGuideOnDeviceModel folder?
folders.answer: **Not by hand.** The folder holds Gemini Nano, the AI model Chrome keeps on your Mac for features like help with writing and scam warnings.
summary: **Not by hand.** The folder holds Gemini Nano, the AI model Chrome keeps on your Mac for features like help with writing and scam warnings. Deleting it doesn’t break Chrome, but Google says that isn’t the supported way and it may not stop the model coming back.
**What it costs you:** switching the model off removes the Chrome features that depend on it. Browsing, sync and your profile carry on as before.
**Does it come back?** After a manual delete it can, while On-device AI is on. Turn that off in Chrome’s **Settings › AI Innovations** and Chrome deletes the model and stops downloading it.
folders.comes_back: After a manual delete it can, while On-device AI is on. Turn that off in Chrome’s **Settings › AI Innovations** and Chrome deletes the model and stops downloading it.
folders.what: `OptGuideOnDeviceModel` is where Chrome stores **Gemini Nano**, Google’s small language model that runs on your own Mac instead of on Google’s servers. Google lists features that may use it: help with writing or rephrasing text, scam warnings, webpage summaries and tab organisation. Some of Chrome’s AI features don’t rely on it and keep working without it.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Open Chrome, click **More** (the three dots at the top right), then **Settings**.
2. Choose **AI Innovations**.
3. Turn **On-device AI** off.

Chrome then deletes the on-device AI model files and won’t download them again while the setting stays off. Turning it back on brings the features back, and the model downloads again.

Google calls this setting the only supported way to manage the models and says that finding and deleting the files manually is not recommended. If you don’t see AI Innovations, update Chrome first.

folders.name: Claude Code’s ~/.claude folder
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Claude Code’s ~/.claude folder?
folders.answer: **No, not all of it.**
summary: **No, not all of it.** Next to its session transcripts, `~/.claude` holds Claude Code’s settings, your global CLAUDE.md, skills, agents and plugins. Transcripts and logs can go; the configuration is yours and doesn’t come back.

**What it costs you:** deleted transcripts can’t be resumed or rewound, and deleting a whole project folder also takes Claude’s auto memory for that project. Debug logs, plans and shell snapshots cost nothing.
**Does it come back?** New data is written as you use Claude Code; deleted transcripts and settings aren’t. Claude Code already deletes transcripts older than 30 days on its own.
folders.comes_back: New data is written as you use Claude Code; deleted transcripts and settings aren’t. Claude Code already deletes transcripts older than 30 days on its own.
folders.what: Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent for the terminal and editors, keeps everything personal in `~/.claude`. Its documentation splits the folder into two kinds of files:
folders.how_to_clear:
**Let Claude Code do it.** After a session starts, it runs a background sweep that deletes transcripts and other session data older than `cleanupPeriodDays`, 30 by default. To keep less, set a lower number in `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```
{
  "cleanupPeriodDays": 14
}
```

**Remove one project’s history** with `claude purge`. It prints what it will delete and asks first: that project’s transcripts and auto memory, its tasks, debug and file-history entries, its lines in `history.jsonl`, and its entry in `~/.claude.json`. Versions before v2.1.288 call it `claude project purge`.

```
claude purge ~/path/to/project --dry-run
claude purge ~/path/to/project
```

**By hand**, with Claude Code quit: Anthropic’s documentation says deleting `debug`, `plans`, `session-env` and `shell-snapshots` loses nothing you’d notice, and that the legacy `todos`, `statsig`, `logs` and `image-cache` folders aren’t used by current versions. Old transcripts in `projects` can go too, if you won’t resume them; keep each project’s `memory` folder.

> Don’t delete `~/.claude.json`, `~/.claude/settings.json` or `~/.claude/plugins`; Anthropic’s documentation says they hold your account details, preferences and installed plugins. It also lists `.credentials.json` and `agent-memory` among the state files to keep.

folders.name: CocoaPods’ cache and Pods
folders.question: Is it safe to delete CocoaPods’ cache and a project’s Pods folder?
folders.answer: **Yes**, all three come back with `pod install`.
summary: **Yes**, all three come back with `pod install`. The cache is downloads, `~/.cocoapods/repos` is spec indexes, and `Pods` is what `pod install` set up for one project. Keep `Podfile` and `Podfile.lock`.
**What it costs you:** the project won’t build until you run `pod install`, which downloads whatever is no longer cached.
**Does it come back?** Yes, at the versions recorded in `Podfile.lock`.
folders.comes_back: Yes, at the versions recorded in `Podfile.lock`.
folders.what: `Podfile.lock` records the version of each pod that was installed, and `pod install` downloads exactly those versions without checking for newer ones. That’s what makes a deleted `Pods` folder come back as it was.
folders.how_to_clear:
### The download cache

```
pod cache clean --all
```

Without a pod name, `--all` is required, so the whole cache can’t be emptied by accident. `pod cache clean <name>` removes a single pod.

### The old master specs repo

If `pod repo list` shows `master` and your `Podfile` uses the CDN source or names no source at all, remove it:

```
pod repo remove master
```

### A project’s Pods folder

Close the workspace in Xcode, then check Git. CocoaPods recommends keeping `Pods` under source control, so in many projects Git tracks it: deleting it shows up as changes, and `git restore Pods` brings it back. If it’s ignored, delete it and reinstall:

```
rm -rf ~/Projects/MyApp/Pods
cd ~/Projects/MyApp
pod install
```

folders.name: Codex’s ~/.codex folder
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Codex’s ~/.codex folder?
folders.answer: **Partly.** `~/.codex` is the Codex CLI’s home: your `config.toml`, possibly your login, and every session it has saved.
summary: **Partly.** `~/.codex` is the Codex CLI’s home: your `config.toml`, possibly your login, and every session it has saved. Old session transcripts can go if you won’t resume them; the configuration and login are yours to keep.
**What it costs you:** a deleted session can’t be resumed or read back. Deleting `auth.json` signs you out, and deleting `config.toml` resets your settings.
**Does it come back?** New sessions are written as you work. Deleted ones don’t come back, and Codex keeps every session until you archive or delete it.
folders.comes_back: New sessions are written as you work. Deleted ones don’t come back, and Codex keeps every session until you archive or delete it.
folders.what: OpenAI’s Codex CLI keeps its local state in `CODEX_HOME`, which is `~/.codex` unless you set it elsewhere. OpenAI lists what you may find there:
folders.how_to_clear:
**Use Codex’s own command.** `codex delete` permanently deletes a saved session by its ID or name, after asking. The ID is the last part of the session file’s name:

```
codex delete <session>
```

`codex archive` is not the same: OpenAI describes it as tidying the session picker without deleting the transcript, so an archived session still takes its space.

**Old sessions by hand.** With Codex not running, you can move a month’s folder in `~/.codex/sessions` to the Trash in Finder once you’re sure you won’t look back at those sessions.

**Cap the history file.** In `config.toml`, OpenAI’s documentation shows a size limit for the history, after which Codex drops the oldest entries, or a setting that turns history off:

```
[history]
max_bytes = 104857600
# or turn it off: persistence = "none"
```

Leave `config.toml` and `auth.json` alone unless you mean to reset Codex or sign out.

folders.name: conda’s pkgs and environments
folders.question: Is it safe to delete conda’s pkgs folder and old environments?
folders.answer: **Yes, through conda.** `conda clean --all` removes cached packages no environment uses, along with tarballs, index caches and logs.
summary: **Yes, through conda.** `conda clean --all` removes cached packages no environment uses, along with tarballs, index caches and logs. Deleting `pkgs` by hand can break environments that link back to it, so don’t.
**What it costs you:** a package removed from the cache downloads again the next time an environment needs it.
**Does it come back?** The cache refills as you install. Environments are different: one you remove is gone unless you exported it first.
folders.comes_back: The cache refills as you install. Environments are different: one you remove is gone unless you exported it first.
folders.what: conda downloads each package as an archive, unpacks it into its package cache, `pkgs`, and then links the files into every environment that uses it. When the cache and the environments are on the same disk, those are hard links: one file on disk with two names. A package shared by five environments takes its space once.

du -sh "$(conda info --base)"
du -sh "$(conda info --base)/pkgs"
conda clean --all --dry-run
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Close Jupyter, editors and terminals that are using a conda environment.
2. Preview, then clean. `conda clean --all` removes the index cache, unused cached packages, tarballs, temporary files and log files.
3. Leave out `--force-pkgs-dirs` (`-f`). It isn’t part of `--all`: it removes every writable package cache, and conda’s docs warn it breaks environments installed with symlinks back to that cache.

```
conda clean --all --dry-run
conda clean --all
```

conda only checks environments it knows about. Ones that `conda info --envs` doesn’t list aren’t checked for links back to the cache, so make sure yours show up before cleaning.

### Old environments

Environments are yours: conda can’t rebuild one unless you saved what was in it. For each one you might want again, export it, then remove it:

```
conda env export --name old-env --from-history > old-env.yml
conda remove --name old-env --all
```

`--from-history` saves only the packages you asked for, which makes a file that works across platforms. To bring it back later, conda’s docs recommend `conda create --file old-env.yml`; the older `conda env create --file old-env.yml` still works. After removing environments, run `conda clean --all` again, since packages only they used are now unused.

folders.name: Sandboxed apps’ data (Containers)
folders.question: Can I delete ~/Library/Containers on a Mac?
folders.answer: **No, not the folder, and not the container of an app you use.**
summary: **No, not the folder, and not the container of an app you use.** Each container holds everything one sandboxed app keeps: its documents, settings, caches and databases. Deleting one is like reinstalling that app from scratch, and anything saved only inside it is lost.
**The exception:** the container of an app you’ve deleted and won’t use again. Removing an app doesn’t remove its container, so that one is a leftover, once you’ve checked nothing in it is yours.
**Does it come back?** As a fresh, empty container the next time the app opens; the old contents don’t.
folders.comes_back: As a fresh, empty container the next time the app opens; the old contents don’t.
folders.what: Apps from the App Store, and other apps that use Apple’s App Sandbox, can’t write wherever they like. The first time such an app opens, macOS creates a container for it in `~/Library/Containers` and gives the app full access to that folder, with only limited access elsewhere.
folders.how_to_clear:
For an app you use, free space from inside the app rather than deleting its container: remove downloads, old projects or offline content in its settings, and for Docker, use `docker system prune` instead of touching its files.

For an app you’ve removed:

1. Make sure the app is really gone: not in Applications, not in `~/Applications`, and not about to be reinstalled from the App Store.
2. Open its container in Finder and look in `Data/Documents` and `Data/Library/Application Support` for anything of yours, such as exports or saved files. Copy out what you want to keep.
3. Move the container to the Trash; macOS may ask for permission first. Empty the Trash when you’re sure.

If the app has an uninstaller or its maker publishes removal steps, follow those instead: they name the exact folders. Leave the Containers folder itself alone, and Apple’s own `com.apple.…` containers, such as Mail’s.

folders.answer: **No, not by hand.**

2. Find an extension you don’t use, select it and choose Uninstall.

folders.answer: **Yes, once you’ve checked it.**
summary: **Yes, once you’ve checked it.** When an account is deleted and its home folder saved in a disk image, macOS puts that image here. It’s an archive of that person’s files, and nothing on the Mac uses it.
**What it costs you:** possibly the only copy of that account’s documents, photos and mail. Open the image and look before you delete it.

2. Look through Documents, Desktop, Pictures and Downloads for anything someone still wants, and copy it to your own folders or an external drive.

2. Select the reports you don’t need and choose File › Move to Trash.
3. Empty the Trash.

folders.name: Docker Desktop’s Docker.raw
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Docker.raw?
folders.answer: **No, not as a way to free space.**
summary: **No, not as a way to free space.** Docker.raw is the disk of Docker Desktop’s Linux virtual machine. Deleting it removes every image, container and volume at once, databases kept in volumes included, and it must never be deleted while Docker is running.
**What it costs you:** freeing space the right way, with Docker’s own prune commands, costs only images and build cache that download or build again. Deleting the file costs everything inside it.
**Does it come back?** Docker Desktop starts again with an empty disk. What was in it doesn’t come back.
folders.comes_back: Docker Desktop starts again with an empty disk. What was in it doesn’t come back.
folders.what: Containers need Linux, so Docker Desktop for Mac runs a small Linux virtual machine, and Docker’s documentation describes how it stores Linux containers and images in a single large disk image file. That file is Docker.raw. Everything Docker keeps lives inside it:
measure:
docker system df
docker system df -v
folders.how_to_clear:
Free space inside the file with Docker’s own commands, with Docker Desktop running:

```
docker system prune
docker image prune -a
docker builder prune
```

- `docker system prune` removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and build cache. It asks first, and volumes aren’t pruned.
- `docker image prune -a` removes every image no container uses. They download or build again when you need them.
- `docker builder prune` clears build cache only.

Volumes only go if you ask: `docker system prune --volumes` adds unused *anonymous* volumes, and named volumes are only removed by `docker volume prune -a`. Run `docker volume ls` and back up anything you need before using either.

Docker’s FAQ notes that space is only freed when images are deleted, and gives a command that makes Docker hand the freed space back to macOS straight away:

```
docker run --privileged --pid=host docker/desktop-reclaim-space
```

To stop the file growing as large again, lower the disk limit in Settings › Resources › Advanced. Docker warns that lowering it deletes the current disk image, so every container and image in it is lost: prune and back up first.

> To start from empty on purpose, use Docker Desktop’s own reset, Troubleshoot › Clean up data, which destroys all containers and images and keeps your settings. Never delete Docker.raw while Docker Desktop is running.

docker image prune -a
docker builder prune

folders.answer: **Leave the folder itself.**
summary: **Leave the folder itself.** It’s the database of past versions macOS keeps for documents you edit in apps that save automatically, such as Pages, Numbers, Keynote, TextEdit and Preview. Deleting it destroys every saved version at once, and nothing inside can be removed piece by piece by hand.
**What you can do:** delete versions you don’t need from inside the app with File › Revert To, or drop every version of one big document by duplicating it.
**Does it come back?** Yes: macOS keeps saving versions as you work, every hour and whenever you save, rename or duplicate a document.
folders.comes_back: Yes: macOS keeps saving versions as you work, every hour and whenever you save, rename or duplicate a document.
folders.what: Apps that use macOS’s autosave keep a new version of a document every hour, or more often while you’re making lots of changes, and also whenever you open, save, duplicate, lock, rename or revert it. You see them with File › Revert To › Browse All Versions, in a timeline beside the current document.
folders.how_to_clear:
Delete versions you don’t need, one document at a time:

1. Open the document and choose File › Revert To › Browse All Versions.
2. Click along the timeline to a version you don’t need.
3. Move the pointer to the top of the screen to show the menu bar, then choose File › Revert To › Delete This Version.

To drop every old version of one large document at once, select it in Finder, choose File › Duplicate, delete the original, and give the copy the original’s name. The duplicate starts with no versions. Restart afterwards to give macOS a chance to tidy its store.

Don’t remove the folder, or anything in it, with `sudo rm`. Besides losing every version, taking pieces out leaves the database out of step with what it stores.

folders.name: ._ files (AppleDouble) and dot_clean
folders.question: Is it safe to delete ._ files, and what does dot_clean do?
folders.answer: **Yes**, on a drive that goes into a TV, car stereo, camera or Windows PC.
summary: **Yes**, on a drive that goes into a TV, car stereo, camera or Windows PC. A `._` file holds only Mac extras for the file of the same name, such as Finder tags and the quarantine flag, never the file’s contents.

**What it costs you:** those extras, for the files whose `._` partner you remove. For music, photos and videos that’s nothing you’d miss; very old Mac files that keep data in a resource fork can stop working.
**Does it come back?** Yes, whenever a Mac copies or changes files on that drive again. `dot_clean`, built into macOS, clears them.
folders.comes_back: Yes, whenever a Mac copies or changes files on that drive again. `dot_clean`, built into macOS, clears them.
folders.what: Mac files can carry information beside their contents: extended attributes such as Finder tags and the flag that marks a file as downloaded from the internet, Finder info, and on old files a resource fork. APFS and Mac OS Extended store all that inside the file system. A drive formatted ExFAT or FAT32 has nowhere to put it, so macOS writes it to a separate file with the same name and `._` in front, in a format called AppleDouble. Apple’s engineers describe zip archives the same way: a format with no place for Mac metadata gets AppleDouble files.
measure:
find /Volumes/MyDrive -name '._*' -type f | wc -l
find /Volumes/MyDrive -name '._*' -type f -exec du -k {} + | awk '{s+=$1} END {print s " KB"}'
folders.how_to_clear:
`dot_clean` comes with macOS. With the drive connected:

1. Find the drive’s name in Finder’s sidebar. In Terminal it’s `/Volumes/` followed by that name.
2. To remove every `._` file on it, run `dot_clean -m` on the drive. Its manual says `-m` always deletes dot-underscore files.
3. To remove only orphans, the `._` files whose real file was deleted on a TV or a PC, use `-n` instead: it deletes a dot-underscore file only when there’s no matching file.
4. Eject the drive in Finder before unplugging it.

```
dot_clean -m /Volumes/MyDrive
```

Run with no option, `dot_clean` merges each `._` file’s information into its partner file; `-m` also deletes the `._` files, which is what a drive for other devices needs. A zip file’s `__MACOSX` folder can simply go to the Trash after unzipping.

folders.question: Is it safe to delete .DS_Store files?
folders.answer: **Yes.** A `.DS_Store` file only remembers how Finder shows its folder: the view, where icons sit and similar settings.
summary: **Yes.** A `.DS_Store` file only remembers how Finder shows its folder: the view, where icons sit and similar settings. None of your files are inside it.
**What it costs you:** that folder opens with Finder’s default view until you arrange it again. Each file is a few kilobytes, so there’s no real space to win.
**Does it come back?** Yes. Finder writes a new one when it opens the folder again, so clearing them is mainly for folders you share.
folders.comes_back: Yes. Finder writes a new one when it opens the folder again, so clearing them is mainly for folders you share.
folders.what: The name stands for Desktop Services Store. Finder creates one in folders it opens and keeps that folder’s view options, icon positions and other visual information in it. 2. **A USB drive or SD card:** close any Finder window showing it, run the same command on `/Volumes/` followed by the drive’s name, then eject it.
3. **A Git repository:** add `.DS_Store` to Git’s global ignore file so it’s never committed again, and remove any already committed with `git rm --cached .DS_Store`.

```
find /Volumes/MyDrive -name .DS_Store -type f -delete
```

```
mkdir -p ~/.config/git && echo .DS_Store >> ~/.config/git/ignore
```

Git uses `~/.config/git/ignore` as its global ignore file by default, unless `core.excludesFile` or `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` points somewhere else. For network shares, Apple documents a setting that stops Finder using `.DS_Store` files on SMB shares; log out and back in after running it:

folders.question: Can I delete dyld (the dyld shared cache) on a Mac?
folders.answer: **No.** The dyld shared cache is where macOS keeps all of its system libraries, the code every app on your Mac runs on.
summary: **No.** The dyld shared cache is where macOS keeps all of its system libraries, the code every app on your Mac runs on. Since macOS 11 those libraries no longer exist as separate files, so this cache is the only copy.
**What deleting it would cost:** apps, and macOS itself, couldn’t start. That’s why it lives in parts of the system that are sealed and checked, where you can’t change it.

folders.comes_back: It’s replaced with each macOS update and never needs cleaning by hand. There’s nothing to win here.

- Count it as part of macOS, like the rest of the system. Its size is set by Apple and changes with updates.

folders.name: Font caches
folders.question: Is it safe to delete the font caches on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Yes**, with Apple’s tools.
summary: **Yes**, with Apple’s tools. Font caches are databases macOS builds from the fonts you have installed, so resetting them deletes no fonts. It’s a repair for fonts that misbehave, not a way to free space.
**What it costs you:** a restart or a log out, and some Font Book choices to redo: fonts you turned off can be back on, and fonts you activated from other folders may need activating again.
**Does it come back?** Yes. macOS builds new databases from the fonts in the standard font folders after you log out or restart.
folders.comes_back: Yes. macOS builds new databases from the fonts in the standard font folders after you log out or restart.
folders.what: Every app that draws text asks macOS which fonts exist, where their files are and which ones are turned on. Rather than read every font file each time, macOS’s font service, `fontd`, keeps a registry: databases and cache files built from the fonts in the standard font folders, plus your choices in Font Book.
folders.how_to_clear:
Start with the gentlest step that fixes the problem:

1. **Check the fonts first.** In Font Book, select fonts and choose File › Validate Selection. Fonts that fail show in red, and you can remove them with Remove Checked. File › Resolve Duplicates deals with two copies of the same font.
2. **Start up in safe mode.** Apple says safe mode clears some system caches, including font caches, which macOS creates again as needed. Start up in safe mode, then restart normally and look at the fonts again.
3. **Reset your own font caches from Terminal.** Quit your apps, run `atsutil databases -removeUser`, then log out and back in, or restart.

```
atsutil databases -removeUser
```

Its manual says `-removeUser` removes the font databases for the active user only, which is enough for a problem in your own account; `-remove` clears the system’s databases as well. Older guides also tell you to run `atsutil server -shutdown` and `atsutil server -ping`. folders.name: File change logs (.fseventsd)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete .fseventsd on a Mac?
folders.answer: **No, leave it.** `.fseventsd` is macOS’s running record of which folders changed on a disk.
summary: **No, leave it.** `.fseventsd` is macOS’s running record of which folders changed on a disk. Backup and sync tools use it to catch up on changes without rescanning everything.
**What deleting it costs:** the tools that rely on that history lose it, and may have to scan the whole disk to work out what changed. Apple tells developers never to work with these files directly.
**Does it come back?** At once: macOS’s `fseventsd` service keeps writing it as files change.
folders.comes_back: At once: macOS’s `fseventsd` service keeps writing it as files change.
folders.what: Whenever files are created, changed or deleted, macOS notes which folder it happened in. Apps can ask to hear about changes as they happen, and can also ask what changed since a point in the past, even if they weren’t running at the time. Apple’s own example is a backup app working out which files have changed since its last run.
folders.how_to_clear:
On your Mac’s own disk, leave it. Deleting it gains little and throws away the change history that backup and sync apps depend on. Apple even tells developers not to purge event history, because no app can assume it’s the only one using it.

On an external drive it does no harm either: other computers ignore it, and a Mac creates it again. Apple’s old developer guide describes switching logging off for a volume with an empty file named `no_log` inside `.fseventsd`, meant for cases like backup volumes. An Apple engineer has since said he wouldn’t recommend opting general-purpose volumes out, and a developer reported that it no longer seemed to work on an APFS volume in macOS 15.5.

folders.name: A project’s .git folder
folders.question: Is it safe to delete a project’s .git folder?
folders.answer: **Usually not.** `.git` is the repository itself: every commit, branch, tag and stash of the project.
summary: **Usually not.** `.git` is the repository itself: every commit, branch, tag and stash of the project. Your current files stay if you delete it, but the folder stops being a Git repository.

**What it costs you:** anything that exists only on this Mac: commits you haven’t pushed, local branches, stashes, and the whole history of a project that never had a remote. If everything is pushed, cloning again gets it all back.
**Does it come back?** Only by cloning from a remote, and only what you pushed. To get space back, make the repository smaller with Git’s own tools instead.
folders.comes_back: Only by cloning from a remote, and only what you pushed. To get space back, make the repository smaller with Git’s own tools instead.
folders.what: When you run `git init` or `git clone`, Git creates a hidden `.git` folder at the top of the project. That folder is the repository. The files you edit are one checked-out version of what’s stored inside it.
folders.how_to_clear:
**To make it smaller, keep it and tidy it.** Git already runs `git gc` automatically when a repository has grown a lot, but you can run it yourself, for example after deleting many branches:

```
git gc
```

It compresses file revisions and removes unreachable objects older than a grace period, two weeks by default. Git’s documentation says `--aggressive` isn’t worth it for most repositories, and warns that `--prune=now` can corrupt a repository if another Git process is writing to it at the same time. In projects using Git LFS, `git lfs prune --dry-run` shows which old local copies it would delete; files referenced by commits you haven’t pushed are kept.

**To drop the history of a project you’re done with**, first make sure nothing exists only here:

```
git status
git stash list
git log --branches --not --remotes --oneline
```

The last command lists commits on local branches that no remote has. If all three come back empty, deleting the project and cloning it again later loses nothing you’ve pushed. To keep the files but drop the history, quit editors using the project and move `.git` to the Trash, which lets you change your mind until you empty it.

folders.name: Go’s module and build caches
folders.question: Is it safe to delete ~/go/pkg/mod and Go’s build cache?
folders.answer: **Yes**, with Go’s own commands.
summary: **Yes**, with Go’s own commands. The module cache holds downloaded dependencies and the build cache holds compiled packages, and both come back. Use `go clean`, because module files are read-only and `rm -rf` fails on them.
**What it costs you:** the next build downloads modules again and compiles from scratch.
**Does it come back?** Yes. The build cache trims itself; the module cache only grows until you clean it.
folders.comes_back: Yes. The build cache trims itself; the module cache only grows until you clean it.
folders.what: Go creates module files and folders read-only so tests and editors can’t change a dependency after it was checked against `go.sum`. That protection is also why deleting the folder by hand fails with permission errors.
folders.how_to_clear:
```
go clean -modcache
go clean -cache
```

- `go clean -modcache` removes the entire module cache, unpacked source included. Go’s reference calls it usually the best way, because it deals with the read-only permissions for you.
- `go clean -cache` removes the entire build cache.
- `go clean -testcache` only expires cached test results, if stale passes are the problem.
- Leave `go clean -fuzzcache` alone unless you mean it: it deletes inputs the fuzzer found that expand coverage, which makes fuzzing less effective.

If you’d rather `rm -rf` worked in future, `go env -w GOFLAGS=-modcacherw` makes new module folders writable. Go’s docs ask for caution with it, since writable modules can be changed by accident; `go mod verify` detects such changes.

folders.question: Is it safe to delete Google Drive for desktop’s DriveFS folder?
folders.answer: **Leave it.** `DriveFS` is Google Drive for desktop’s cache, and Google’s admin documentation says files are moved there before they’re uploaded.
summary: **Leave it.** `DriveFS` is Google Drive for desktop’s cache, and Google’s admin documentation says files are moved there before they’re uploaded. Delete it while something is waiting to upload and that change can be lost.

### Stream instead of mirror

1. Open Drive for desktop and make sure your local files have finished syncing.
2. Click **Settings**, then **Preferences**.

Streamed files are online-only unless they were made available offline through Drive for desktop, so turn that off for folders you don’t need without a connection.

folders.name: Gradle’s caches (~/.gradle)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Gradle’s caches in ~/.gradle?
folders.answer: **Yes**, with Gradle stopped.
summary: **Yes**, with Gradle stopped. `caches`, `wrapper/dists`, `jdks` and the daemon logs are downloads and build data Gradle fetches or makes again. Keep `gradle.properties` and `init.d`: those are your settings.
**What it costs you:** the next build downloads dependencies, and perhaps a Gradle distribution and a JDK, before it starts, so it runs slower that once.
**Does it come back?** Yes. Gradle also prunes these folders itself, so clearing by hand is mainly for getting space back now.
folders.comes_back: Yes. Gradle also prunes these folders itself, so clearing by hand is mainly for getting space back now.
folders.what: `~/.gradle` is the Gradle User Home, shared by every Gradle and Android project you build, from Terminal or from Android Studio and IntelliJ IDEA. Gradle’s docs list what lives there:

1. Quit Android Studio or IntelliJ IDEA, and let running builds finish.
2. Stop the daemons with `./gradlew --stop` in a project, or `gradle --stop`. Each stops only daemons of its own Gradle version; others shut themselves down after 3 idle hours, and `gradle --status` lists those of the current version.
3. Clear the caches, then look at which distributions you have.

```
./gradlew --stop
rm -rf ~/.gradle/caches/*
ls ~/.gradle/wrapper/dists
```

Delete a version folder in `wrapper/dists` only if no project still uses that Gradle version; otherwise that project’s next `./gradlew` downloads it again. Leave `gradle.properties`, which can hold signing settings and repository credentials, and `init.d` alone.

A project’s `build` folder is its output: the `clean` task deletes the build directory, and the next build makes it again. The project’s `.gradle` folder is Gradle’s per-project cache, with build state for incremental builds and the configuration cache; it can go too, with Gradle stopped.

```

```

folders.question: Is it safe to delete ~/.cache/huggingface?
folders.answer: **Yes, but pick what goes.**
summary: **Yes, but pick what goes.** It’s where Hugging Face’s Python libraries keep every model and dataset file you’ve downloaded, and they don’t delete any of it themselves. Use `hf cache rm` and `hf cache prune` rather than deleting folders by hand.
**What it costs you:** a fresh download the next time your code loads a model or dataset you removed. Your Hugging Face login token sits in the same folder, so don’t delete the folder whole.
**Does it come back?** Yes: when code asks for a model or dataset that isn’t cached, it downloads it again.
folders.comes_back: Yes: when code asks for a model or dataset that isn’t cached, it downloads it again.
folders.what: `transformers`, `diffusers`, `datasets` and other libraries built on `huggingface_hub` download files from the Hugging Face Hub into one shared cache, so a model fetched by one script is reused by the next. Hugging Face’s documentation is plain about the catch: cached files are never deleted, and when you download a newer revision of a model, the previous files are kept in case you need them again.
measure:
hf cache ls
hf cache ls --revisions --filter "accessed>30d"
du -sh ~/.cache/huggingface/*
folders.how_to_clear:
Remove whole models or datasets you no longer use. `hf cache rm` asks before deleting, and `--dry-run` shows what would go:

```
hf cache rm model/<org>/<name> --dry-run
hf cache rm model/<org>/<name>
```

Then clear the leftovers. `hf cache prune` deletes revisions that no branch or tag points to any more, partial files from interrupted downloads, and shared files no cached repository uses:

```
hf cache prune
```

With older versions, `huggingface-cli delete-cache` opens a list where you tick what to remove.

The CLI is safer than Finder here. Recent versions store some files once, in a shared `blobs` folder at the top of `hub`, for every repository that uses them, and only `hf cache rm` and `hf cache prune` know when those can go. The `xet` folder is the exception: Hugging Face’s docs say you can remove it entirely to reclaim its space.
clear_commands:
hf cache rm model/<org>/<name> --dry-run
hf cache rm model/<org>/<name>

folders.name: iCloud Drive’s local copies
folders.question: Is it safe to delete the local copies of iCloud Drive files?
folders.answer: **Only with Remove Download.**
summary: **Only with Remove Download.** Deleting a file in iCloud Drive, from Finder or from its folder in your Library, deletes it from iCloud and every device signed in to your Apple Account. Removing the download frees the space on this Mac and leaves the file in iCloud.
**What it costs you:** a removed download needs an internet connection, and a moment, the next time you open it.
**Does it come back?** A removed download comes back when you open the file. A deleted file comes back only from Recently Deleted on iCloud.com, for 30 days.
folders.comes_back: A removed download comes back when you open the file. A deleted file comes back only from Recently Deleted on iCloud.com, for 30 days.
folders.what: With iCloud Drive syncing on this Mac, macOS keeps local copies of your iCloud Drive files so they open instantly, and keeps them in step with iCloud. If Desktop & Documents Folders is on, your Desktop and Documents are part of iCloud Drive as well.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. **Free space here, keep the file in iCloud:** in Finder, Control-click a file or folder in iCloud Drive and choose **Remove Download**. It stays listed, marked as in iCloud, and downloads again when you open it.
2. **Let macOS do it as space runs out:** System Settings › your name › iCloud › Drive, check that Sync this Mac is on, turn on **Optimize Mac Storage**, and click Done. Apple says your Mac can then store documents in iCloud when more space is needed.
3. **Keep some things on the Mac no matter what:** Control-click them and choose Keep Downloaded.
4. **Delete for good:** only for files you don’t want anywhere. Move them to the Trash in Finder; they leave your other devices too, and iCloud.com keeps them in Recently Deleted for 30 days.

> Don’t delete folders inside `~/Library/Mobile Documents` to save space. That deletes the files from iCloud and from every device, not just from this Mac.

folders.name: iMovie render files
folders.question: Is it safe to delete iMovie’s render files?
folders.answer: **Yes, with iMovie’s own Delete button.**
summary: **Yes, with iMovie’s own Delete button.** Render files are versions of your edits iMovie prepares so playback and export run smoothly. Apple says deleting them removes no imported media.
**What it costs you:** some waiting. iMovie renders again as you play and export, and an export that’s running when you delete them may take longer.
**Does it come back?** Yes. iMovie makes new render files as you edit, so they build up again with each project.
folders.comes_back: Yes. iMovie makes new render files as you edit, so they build up again with each project.
folders.what: When you add titles, transitions, effects or slow motion, iMovie works out the result in advance so it can play without stuttering. Those prepared versions are render files. They’re stored inside your iMovie library, alongside the footage, and they’re pure working files: iMovie can always make them again from your clips and edits.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Open iMovie with the library you want to clear. File › Open Library switches to another one.
2. Choose **iMovie › Settings** (⌘,).
3. Next to **Render Files**, click **Delete** and confirm.
4. Quit iMovie and check the library’s size again.

Apple’s description: it removes render files from your open libraries, freeing up storage space, and no imported media is removed. If an export is running, let it finish first.

folders.name: Xcode iOS DeviceSupport
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Xcode’s iOS DeviceSupport folder?
folders.answer: **Yes**, with Xcode quit, and especially the folders for iOS versions none of your devices run any more.
summary: **Yes**, with Xcode quit, and especially the folders for iOS versions none of your devices run any more. They’re copies of system symbols Xcode took from your iPhone or iPad so it could debug apps on it. Your apps, projects and archives aren’t in there.
**What it costs you:** the next time you connect a device whose folder you deleted, Xcode copies its symbols again before it can debug on it, so that first connection takes longer.
**Does it come back?** Yes, for each device you plug in again. Folders for iOS versions you no longer use simply don’t come back.
folders.comes_back: Yes, for each device you plug in again. Folders for iOS versions you no longer use simply don’t come back.
folders.what: To debug an app on an iPhone or iPad, Xcode needs the debug symbols of the exact iOS version on that device, so the debugger can show readable system frames instead of raw addresses. The first time you connect a device running an iOS version Xcode hasn’t seen, it prepares the device for development and copies those symbols to your Mac.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Quit Xcode and disconnect your devices, so nothing is copying symbols while you delete.
2. Open `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/iOS DeviceSupport` in Finder.
3. Move the folders for iOS versions none of your devices run any more to the Trash. Keep the folders that match the devices you debug on now, so you don’t wait for them to be copied again. Then empty the Trash.

Or clear everything inside it from Terminal, with Xcode quit:

```
rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/"iOS DeviceSupport"/*
```

Clearing the whole folder is also one of Apple’s own fixes. When Xcode failed to copy symbols from devices, the Xcode 12.2 release notes gave this workaround: disconnect every device, delete `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/iOS DeviceSupport`, open the Devices and Simulators window, and reconnect each device with a USB cable so Xcode copies its symbols again.

folders.name: iPhone and iPad update files (.ipsw)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete iPhone and iPad software updates (.ipsw files)?
folders.answer: **Yes.** An `.ipsw` file is a copy of iOS or iPadOS your Mac downloaded to update or restore a device.
summary: **Yes.** An `.ipsw` file is a copy of iOS or iPadOS your Mac downloaded to update or restore a device. Once that’s done nothing needs it, and your iPhone backups aren’t in it.
**What it costs you:** a fresh download the next time you update or restore a device from this Mac.
**Does it come back?** Yes, when it’s needed: the Mac downloads the software again for the next update or restore.
folders.comes_back: Yes, when it’s needed: the Mac downloads the software again for the next update or restore.
folders.what: When you update or restore an iPhone or iPad from your Mac, in Finder (or in iTunes on older macOS), the Mac downloads that device’s complete system software as a single `.ipsw` file and installs it from there. Storage settings lists these under **iOS Files**, which Apple describes as iOS backups and firmware; these files are the firmware.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Make sure no update or restore is running; if a device is connected, let Finder finish.
2. Open System Settings › General › Storage, click ⓘ next to iOS Files, select the software files (not the backups) and click Delete.
3. Or open the folder in Finder, drag the `.ipsw` files to the Trash and empty it.

Leave the backups in `~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup` alone unless you mean to delete one: that’s a separate choice, with no undo.

folders.name: JetBrains IDE caches
folders.question: Is it safe to delete ~/Library/Caches/JetBrains?
folders.answer: **Yes**, with the IDE quit.
summary: **Yes**, with the IDE quit. It’s the system folder of IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm and the other JetBrains IDEs: caches they build again from your projects. Folders for IDE versions you no longer use can go any time.

**What it costs you:** the IDE rebuilds its caches when you next open each project, which takes a while for big ones. You also lose Local History, the IDE’s own record of recent file changes, because it lives in this folder too.
**Does it come back?** Yes, as soon as you open a project in that IDE again.
folders.comes_back: Yes, as soon as you open a project in that IDE again.
folders.what: Every JetBrains IDE keeps separate folders for each installed version: configuration and plugins in `~/Library/Application Support/JetBrains`, logs in `~/Library/Logs/JetBrains`, and a **system** folder here, in `~/Library/Caches/JetBrains`. JetBrains describes the system folder as holding caches and Local History.
folders.how_to_clear:
**Old versions first.** In the IDE you use now, choose Help › Delete Leftover IDE Directories… and pick the versions you no longer plan to use. JetBrains IDEs also delete the caches and logs folders of older versions on their own when you install a new major version, if those folders haven’t been updated in the last 180 days.

**The current version’s caches.** Choose File › Invalidate Caches… It removes the cache files for every project you’ve opened in this version of the IDE, and they’re recreated the next time you open those projects. Local History is kept unless you tick the option to clear it.

**By hand**, with every JetBrains IDE quit, to clear the whole folder:

```
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/JetBrains/*
```

That takes Local History with it, for every IDE. If you might need an uncommitted change back, open the project and look in Local History before you clear anything.

folders.name: Keychains folder
folders.question: Is it safe to delete ~/Library/Keychains?
folders.answer: **No.** `~/Library/Keychains` holds your login keychain and this Mac’s copy of your iCloud Keychain or Local Items: saved passwords, passkeys, certificates and private keys.
summary: **No.** `~/Library/Keychains` holds your login keychain and this Mac’s copy of your iCloud Keychain or Local Items: saved passwords, passkeys, certificates and private keys. Deleting it frees almost no space and loses whatever isn’t stored anywhere else.
**What it costs you:** apps and websites ask you to sign in again, and certificates and keys that lived only on this Mac are gone.
**Does it come back?** Not by itself. Passwords you sync with iCloud Keychain are still in iCloud, but anything kept only on this Mac needs a backup to come back.
folders.comes_back: Not by itself. Passwords you sync with iCloud Keychain are still in iCloud, but anything kept only on this Mac needs a backup to come back.
folders.what: A keychain is an encrypted database of secrets that macOS and your apps fill in so you don’t have to type them again: passwords for websites and apps, passkeys, secure notes, certificates and the private keys that go with them. The Passwords app shows your passwords, passkeys and verification codes; Keychain Access shows everything, certificates and keys included.
folders.how_to_clear:
There’s no safe way to delete the folder. What people usually want is one of these, and each has its own tool:

- **Fewer saved passwords:** delete the ones you don’t use in the Passwords app, or select them in Keychain Access and delete them there. With iCloud Keychain on, the change reaches your other devices too.
- **Your Mac keeps asking for the login keychain password:** the keychain password no longer matches your login password, usually after the login password was reset. Apple recommends changing your password in Users & Groups settings so the keychain follows. Only if you don’t remember the old password, reset the default keychain: Keychain Access › Settings › Reset Default Keychains, then log out and back in. Apple warns that this deletes all the passwords saved in the keychain, and recommends doing it only when Apple Support advises it.
- **A keychain you made yourself, or one whose password you’ve forgotten:** in Keychain Access, select it in the Keychains list, choose File › Delete Keychain, and click Delete References.

> Don’t delete `login.keychain-db` or the long-ID folder in Finder to start fresh. You lose every item in them, and macOS has no way to know that’s what you meant.

folders.name: Your caches folder (~/Library/Caches)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete ~/Library/Caches on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Yes**, app by app, with each app quit.
summary: **Yes**, app by app, with each app quit. Everything in it is a copy an app can make again: images and web content it already loaded, compiled code, package archives. Your documents, settings and passwords are kept elsewhere.
**What it costs you:** a little speed for a while. Apps open and load more slowly until they’ve rebuilt what they use, and package managers download again what they need.
**Does it come back?** Yes. It starts refilling as soon as you use your apps, so clearing it buys space for a while rather than for good.
folders.comes_back: Yes. It starts refilling as soon as you use your apps, so clearing it buys space for a while rather than for good.
folders.what: `~/Library/Caches` is the cache folder of your own user account. Each app gets a folder inside it, usually named after its app ID, such as `com.spotify.client`, or after the app or tool itself, like `Homebrew` or `pip`. What goes in is up to the app: thumbnails, web content, downloaded updates, compiled shaders, package archives.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Find the big folders with the command above and work out which app each belongs to. The name usually tells you: `com.google.Chrome` is Chrome, `Homebrew` is Homebrew.
2. Quit that app with `⌘Q`, so nothing is writing to its cache while you clear it.
3. In Finder, open the app’s folder, select everything inside and move it to the Trash. Keep the folder itself, then empty the Trash.

The same in Terminal for one app, with it quit (put the real folder name in):

```
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/com.example.app/*
```

Where a tool has a clean command of its own, use it instead, because it knows what it can drop: `brew cleanup` for Homebrew, `pip cache purge` for pip, `yarn cache clean` for Yarn. Don’t delete `~/Library/Caches` itself, and don’t empty everything at once while apps are open.

folders.name: Log files (~/Library/Logs)
folders.question: Can I delete all the log files on my Mac?
folders.answer: **Yes, your old ones.**
summary: **Yes, your old ones.** Log files record what apps and installers did, and once they’re a week or so old nobody reads them unless something has gone wrong. Clearing old files from your own `~/Library/Logs` is harmless.
**What it costs you:** the history you’d want when chasing a problem. Keep recent logs, and any report a developer has asked you for.

**Does it come back?** New logs appear as apps keep writing; the old ones are gone for good. “All logs” isn’t something you can or need to delete: macOS’s main log is managed by macOS, which trims it itself.
folders.comes_back: New logs appear as apps keep writing; the old ones are gone for good. “All logs” isn’t something you can or need to delete: macOS’s main log is managed by macOS, which trims it itself.
folders.what: A Mac keeps logs in several places, and they aren’t all the same kind:
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Quit the app whose logs you’re clearing, so it isn’t writing to them.
2. In Finder, open `~/Library/Logs` with Go › Go to Folder and move old files, or a whole app’s folder, to the Trash. Leave the `Logs` folder itself.
3. For reports, use Console: select one under Reports and choose File › Move to Trash.
4. Empty the Trash.

In Terminal, first list the files in your own logs that haven’t changed for over a week, then delete exactly those:

```
find ~/Library/Logs -type f -mtime +7 -print
find ~/Library/Logs -type f -mtime +7 -delete
```

Leave `/Library/Logs` and `/private/var/log` to macOS unless one file there has run away; then remove that file in Finder once you’ve dealt with whatever writes it. Don’t try to clear the unified log: Apple says that when its store passes a set size, macOS purges the oldest messages to make room.

folders.name: Lightroom Classic’s previews
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Lightroom Classic’s Previews.lrdata?
folders.answer: **Yes**, with Lightroom Classic quit.
summary: **Yes**, with Lightroom Classic quit. Adobe says it’s safe to delete the previews file as long as its name matches your catalog’s, and Lightroom regenerates previews as you work. Your edits are in the catalog (`.lrcat`), not here.
**What it costs you:** speed. Lightroom is slower until previews are rebuilt, and previews of photos on a disconnected drive are lost until you plug it back in.
**Does it come back?** Yes, folder by folder, as you open them.
folders.comes_back: Yes, folder by folder, as you open them.
folders.what: Lightroom Classic shows your photos from previews it renders and stores in one file next to your catalog, named `[Catalog name] Previews.lrdata`. It holds thumbnails, standard-size previews and 1:1 previews, which have the same pixel dimensions as the originals and show sharpening and noise reduction. The 1:1 previews are the big ones.
folders.how_to_clear:
### Discard 1:1 previews, keep the rest

1. Choose **Lightroom Classic › Catalog Settings** and find **Automatically Discard 1:1 Previews** (under File Handling, or Previews in recent versions).
2. Pick a shorter period, such as a day or a week, instead of 30 days or Never.
3. To discard them now, select photos in the Grid and choose **Library › Previews › Discard 1:1 Previews**.

Recent versions can also cap the whole preview cache in Catalog Settings: once it reaches the size you set, Lightroom purges older previews in the background, but never ones from the last 30 days.

### Delete the whole file

1. Quit Lightroom Classic.
2. In the catalog’s folder, check names: delete only the `Previews.lrdata` that matches your `.lrcat`, and leave `Smart Previews.lrdata` unless you mean it.
3. Move it to the Trash, empty the Trash and open Lightroom.

Adobe suggests deleting it when your disk is unexpectedly full, when Lightroom reports a cache error, or when photos show lines, dots or odd colours that point to corrupt previews.

folders.name: LM Studio models
folders.question: Is it safe to delete LM Studio’s models folder?
folders.answer: **Yes, model by model.**
summary: **Yes, model by model.** Every model you downloaded in LM Studio is a folder of weight files in its models folder, and you can remove the ones you no longer use. Your chats aren’t stored with them: they’re in `~/.lmstudio/conversations`.
**What it costs you:** the model, until you download it again from LM Studio’s Discover tab or with `lms get`.
**Does it come back?** Only by downloading it again.
folders.comes_back: Only by downloading it again.
folders.what: LM Studio is a desktop app for running language models locally, with its own model downloader. Models you get from its Discover tab, or with the `lms get` command, are saved in its models folder, laid out the way Hugging Face lays them out: a folder per publisher, then a folder per model.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Unload the model if it’s loaded, in LM Studio or with `lms unload --all`.
2. Open My Models (`⌘3`) and find the model.
3. Remove it there, and confirm.

Or in Finder, with LM Studio quit: open the models folder My Models shows, go into the publisher’s folder and move the model’s folder to the Trash. `lms ls` reflects what’s in the current models folder, so a model you deleted no longer appears there.

> Leave `~/.lmstudio/conversations` alone unless you mean to delete chats: deleting a model doesn’t touch them, and they don’t come back.

folders.name: Old macOS installers
folders.question: Can I delete old macOS installers and old versions of macOS?
folders.answer: **Yes, the installers.** An app named “Install macOS …” in Applications is a full macOS installer that was downloaded and never removed.
summary: **Yes, the installers.** An app named “Install macOS …” in Applications is a full macOS installer that was downloaded and never removed. It isn’t the macOS your Mac runs, and Apple lets you download it again whenever you need it.
**What it costs you:** nothing, unless you meant to upgrade with it soon or make a bootable USB installer from it. Keep it until you have.
**Does it come back?** Only if you download it again, from Software Update, the App Store or Apple’s download page.
folders.comes_back: Only if you download it again, from Software Update, the App Store or Apple’s download page.
folders.what: A full copy of macOS, downloaded from the App Store, from Apple’s download links or with `softwareupdate --fetch-full-installer`, arrives as an app in Applications named after the version, such as Install macOS Tahoe. Apple’s own instructions say you can quit the installer to leave it in the Applications folder for later use, and people keep one on purpose to make a bootable USB installer. Either way, it can sit there long after it’s needed.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Check which macOS you run: Apple menu › About This Mac.
2. An installer for that version or an older one has nothing left to do. Drag it to the Trash and empty the Trash. If Finder asks for an administrator’s name and password, an administrator account installed it.
3. An installer for a newer macOS you haven’t installed yet: keep it until you upgrade, or delete it and let Software Update download what it needs when you’re ready.
4. Want a bootable USB installer? Make it first with Apple’s `createinstallmedia` steps; Apple’s guide then says you can delete the installer from your Applications folder.

If the installer is open, quit it first. Never try to free space from the macOS part of your disk or anything under `/System`: that’s the system itself, and macOS protects it.

folders.name: Mail’s data folder
folders.question: Is it safe to delete ~/Library/Mail?
folders.answer: **No.** `~/Library/Mail` is Mail’s copy of your email: every mailbox, message and downloaded attachment, including mailboxes kept On My Mac and POP mail that may exist nowhere else.
summary: **No.** `~/Library/Mail` is Mail’s copy of your email: every mailbox, message and downloaded attachment, including mailboxes kept On My Mac and POP mail that may exist nowhere else.
**What it costs you:** anything that was only on this Mac, plus a long download of everything else from your mail servers.
**Does it come back?** Only what’s still on the servers. To make Mail smaller, work from inside Mail with the steps below.
folders.comes_back: Only what’s still on the servers. To make Mail smaller, work from inside Mail with the steps below.
folders.what: Mail keeps your email on the Mac so it can show and search it offline, and that copy is `~/Library/Mail`. Inside is a folder named `V` plus a number for the current storage format (`V10` on recent versions of macOS), holding a folder for each account named by a long ID, a `Mailboxes` folder for mailboxes stored On My Mac, and `MailData`, with Mail’s index of every message.
folders.how_to_clear:
Work from inside Mail, so your servers and other devices stay in step:

1. **Erase what you’ve deleted.** Deleted messages stay until they’re erased: choose Mailbox › Erase Deleted Items and pick an account. In Mail › Settings › Accounts › Mailbox Behaviors, “Erase deleted messages” makes Mail do it on a schedule.
2. **Find the big messages.** Choose View › Sort By › Size, then delete or move the largest ones you don’t need.
3. **Remove attachments you’ve saved elsewhere.** Select the messages and choose Message › Remove Attachments. The messages stay, marked as having had their attachments removed. For IMAP accounts the attachments are deleted from the server too and can’t be retrieved, so save any you need first.
4. **Download fewer attachments.** In Mail › Settings › Accounts › Account Information, set Download Attachments to Recent, which downloads only those received in the past 15 months, or None. Mail always downloads media attachments, such as images, PDFs, video and audio.
5. **Remove an account you don’t use here.** In Mail › Settings › Accounts, select it and click the remove button. Apple says the account’s messages are removed from your Mac and copies remain on the mail server. If you’re not sure everything is on the server, copy what you need to a mailbox you’re keeping first.

> Don’t delete `~/Library/Mail`, a `V10` folder or an account’s folder in Finder. Anything that was only on this Mac is lost, and Mail has to download the rest again.

folders.name: Mail Downloads
folders.question: Is it safe to delete the Mail Downloads folder?
folders.answer: **Yes, for attachments you only opened.**
summary: **Yes, for attachments you only opened.** When you open or preview an attachment, Mail saves a copy here for the app that opens it. The attachment itself stays in the email.
**What it costs you:** nothing, unless you edited one of those copies and saved it in place. Then your edited version exists only here, so move it somewhere safe first.
**Does it come back?** Only for attachments you open again. Mail also clears unedited copies on its own, by default when you delete the email they came from.
folders.comes_back: Only for attachments you open again. Mail also clears unedited copies on its own, by default when you delete the email they came from.
folders.what: Another app can only open an attachment from a real file on disk. So when you double-click a PDF or a Word document in an email, Mail writes a copy into its Mail Downloads folder and the other app opens that copy. Apple calls these attachments temporarily saved in the Mail Downloads folder.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Quit Mail.
2. Open the folder and look for anything you edited and want to keep, such as a form you filled in. Move it to Documents.
3. Select the rest, move it to the Trash, and empty the Trash.

Or in Terminal, with Mail quit, clear what’s inside the folder:

```
rm -rf "$HOME/Library/Containers/com.apple.mail/Data/Library/Mail Downloads/"*
```
