folders.question: Is it safe to delete ~/.npm, npm’s cache?
folders.answer: **Yes.** `~/.npm` only holds copies of packages npm has already downloaded, plus logs and tools fetched by `npx`.
summary: **Yes.** `~/.npm` only holds copies of packages npm has already downloaded, plus logs and tools fetched by `npx`. Your projects, their `node_modules` and your global packages aren’t in it.
**What it costs you:** the next install of each package downloads it again, so that install needs the network and takes longer.
**Does it come back?** Yes. npm adds to it with every install and never removes anything on its own.
folders.comes_back: Yes. npm adds to it with every install and never removes anything on its own.
folders.what: npm keeps a copy of every package tarball and registry answer it fetches, so installing the same version again can skip the download. Entries are stored by a hash of their contents and checked against that hash on the way in and on the way out. A damaged entry is fetched again instead of breaking an install, which is why npm calls its cache self-healing.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Let any `npm install` that’s running finish.
2. For a trim, run `npm cache verify`. It checks the cache, garbage-collects data nothing points to any more, and reports what it removed. Sometimes that’s enough.
3. To empty it, run `npm cache clean --force`. npm asks for `--force` on purpose: its docs say clearing should never be needed for any reason other than getting disk space back.

```
npm cache verify
npm cache clean --force
```

The `_npx` folder can go as well; `npx` downloads a tool again the next time you run it. With npm not running:

```
rm -rf ~/.npm/_npx/*
```

folders.name: Ollama models
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Ollama models in ~/.ollama/models?
folders.answer: **Yes, with `ollama rm`.**
summary: **Yes, with `ollama rm`.** Each model you pulled is stored as layers in `~/.ollama/models`, and models can share layers. Ollama’s own command frees what only that model used; deleting files in Finder can break the models you keep.
**What it costs you:** the model, until you pull it again, which means downloading it again. A model you built with `ollama create` comes back only if you still have its Modelfile.
**Does it come back?** Only with `ollama pull`. Layers another model still uses are already on your Mac and don’t download again.
folders.comes_back: Only with `ollama pull`. Layers another model still uses are already on your Mac and don’t download again.
folders.what: Ollama runs open-weight language models on your Mac. Every model you fetch with `ollama pull` or `ollama run` is downloaded once and kept until you remove it, so the folder only grows as you try new models.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Check what’s loaded with `ollama ps`, and stop a model you’re about to remove with `ollama stop <model>`.
2. List your models with `ollama list` and pick the ones you no longer use.
3. Remove each one by its full name, tag included.

```
ollama rm <model>:<tag>
```

Ollama deletes the model’s manifest and any layers no other model refers to. Layers still used by another model stay, so that model keeps working.

Don’t delete files in `blobs` by hand: a blob may belong to several models, and a model whose layers are missing can’t load. To start again from nothing, remove every model with `ollama rm` and check that `ollama list` is empty.

Ollama also tidies `blobs` for you: when it starts, it removes blobs that no model refers to any more, such as parts of an interrupted download, unless the `OLLAMA_NOPRUNE` variable is set.

folders.question: Is it safe to delete a Parallels virtual machine (.pvm)?
folders.answer: **Yes, if** you’re done with everything inside it.
summary: **Yes, if** you’re done with everything inside it. A `.pvm` is a whole virtual computer: Windows or Linux, its programs and every file saved in it. Remove it from Parallels’ Control Center; to keep it but take less space, use Parallels’ own Free Up Disk Space.
**What it costs you:** everything in the guest that isn’t saved somewhere else, such as documents kept in Windows, installed programs and their settings. Parallels calls Move to Trash irreversible.

folders.answer: **No, not the library itself.**
summary: **No, not the library itself.** `Photos Library.photoslibrary` is every photo and video in the Photos app, with your albums and edits. Deleting it, or files inside it, can lose pictures that exist nowhere else.

folders.answer: **Yes, by pruning it.**
summary: **Yes, by pruning it.** `pnpm store prune` removes packages no project on your Mac still uses, and pnpm’s docs call it harmless. Deleting the whole store by hand gains little and can bite.

folders.question: Can I delete .plist files in ~/Library/Preferences?
folders.answer: **Not all of them.**
summary: **Not all of them.** Each `.plist` holds one app’s settings, and macOS keeps its own there too, for the Dock, Finder, keyboard and much more. Deleting the lot resets every app and much of macOS to defaults, for very little space.
**What one costs you:** that app’s settings. Resetting a single app is a standard fix when it misbehaves, and the reliable way is the `defaults` command with the app quit.
**Does it come back?** A fresh file with default settings appears as soon as the app runs again; your old choices don’t.
folders.comes_back: A fresh file with default settings appears as soon as the app runs again; your old choices don’t.
folders.what: A property list, or `.plist`, is a small structured file in XML or binary form. Apps rarely touch them directly: macOS’s preferences service, `cfprefsd`, reads an app’s settings when it starts, keeps them in memory while it runs, and writes changes back to the file.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Quit the app, and any helper it keeps running in the menu bar.
2. Find its ID. It’s the file’s name without `.plist`, or Spotlight’s metadata can tell you, as in the first command below.
3. Delete its settings with `defaults delete` and that ID. Going through macOS’s preferences service means a copy held in memory can’t write the old settings back.
4. Open the app. It starts with default settings.

```
mdls -name kMDItemCFBundleIdentifier /Applications/App.app
defaults delete com.example.app
```

In Finder, the equivalent is moving that single `.plist` to the Trash with the app quit. Don’t delete `com.apple.…` files to tidy up, and don’t empty the folder: that resets Dock layouts, Finder views, keyboard shortcuts and accessibility settings in one go.

folders.name: __pycache__ folders
folders.question: Is it safe to delete __pycache__ folders?
folders.answer: **Yes.** Every file in `__pycache__` is compiled from a `.py` file beside it, and Python compiles it again by itself.
summary: **Yes.** Every file in `__pycache__` is compiled from a `.py` file beside it, and Python compiles it again by itself. Nothing in there is the only copy of your code.
**What it costs you:** the next import of each module is a little slower while Python compiles it again. Code doesn’t run slower once it’s loaded.
**Does it come back?** Yes, as soon as the code runs again, unless you tell Python not to write these files.
folders.comes_back: Yes, as soon as the code runs again, unless you tell Python not to write these files.
folders.what: When Python imports a module, it compiles the source to bytecode and saves the result in a `__pycache__` folder next to the `.py` file. The file name carries the module and the Python version, like `spam.cpython-33.pyc` in Python’s own example, so several Python versions can keep their files side by side.
folders.how_to_clear:
From the top of a project, this removes every `__pycache__` folder under it and nothing else:

```
cd ~/Projects/my-app
find . -type d -name __pycache__ -prune -exec rm -rf {} +
```

Run it inside the project folder, never from your home folder or `/`, and run the `find` part on its own first if you want to see the list. Python programs already running carry on; their modules are loaded.

### Stopping them from appearing

- `python -B`, or `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` in your environment, tells Python not to write `.pyc` files on import. Imports then compile every time.
- `PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX`, in Python 3.8 and later, keeps the files but writes them to a mirror tree in one folder instead of `__pycache__` folders in your code.

```
export PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX="$HOME/Library/Caches/pycache"
```

folders.question: Is it safe to delete a Python virtual environment (.venv)?
folders.answer: **Yes**, if the project lists its packages.
summary: **Yes**, if the project lists its packages. Python’s own documentation calls virtual environments disposable: something you delete and recreate from scratch, with no project code inside.
**What it costs you:** one reinstall before the project runs again, which downloads or copies its packages back.
**Does it come back?** Yes, when you recreate it from `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml` or a lockfile.
folders.comes_back: Yes, when you recreate it from `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml` or a lockfile.
folders.what: A virtual environment is a folder with its own `bin/python` and its own `site-packages`, so one project’s packages don’t collide with another’s. You make one with `python3 -m venv .venv`, or a tool such as uv makes it for you. Its `pyvenv.cfg` file records the Python it was created from.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Make sure the project can rebuild it: look for `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, `poetry.lock`, `Pipfile` or `environment.yml`.
2. If there’s no such file, save one from the environment first, with the command below.
3. Run `deactivate` in any terminal that has it active, and quit Jupyter or editors using it.
4. Delete the folder by its full path.

```
.venv/bin/python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
rm -rf ~/Projects/my-app/.venv
```

### Recreating it

```
python3 -m venv .venv
```

folders.name: Quick Look’s thumbnail cache
folders.question: Is it safe to delete the Quick Look thumbnail cache?
folders.answer: **Yes.** It holds the little previews Finder shows instead of plain icons for photos, PDFs, videos and documents.
summary: **Yes.** It holds the little previews Finder shows instead of plain icons for photos, PDFs, videos and documents. Resetting it with Apple’s `qlmanage -r cache` loses nothing you made.
**What it costs you:** a moment of generic icons the next time you open a folder full of pictures, while the previews are drawn again.
**Does it come back?** Yes, by itself. Quick Look makes new thumbnails as you browse, so the cache fills up again.
folders.comes_back: Yes, by itself. Quick Look makes new thumbnails as you browse, so the cache fills up again.
folders.what: When Finder shows a photo, a PDF or a film as a small picture of its contents, that picture comes from **Quick Look**, the part of macOS that also previews a file when you select it and press Space. Drawing a thumbnail means opening the file, so macOS keeps each one it makes in a cache. The next time you open that folder, the icons appear straight away instead of being drawn again.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Open Terminal (in Applications › Utilities).
2. Run `qlmanage -r cache`. It resets the thumbnail cache for your account, with no password to enter and no restart needed.
3. If previews of one kind of file look broken as well, also run `qlmanage -r`, which reloads Quick Look’s list of generators.

```
qlmanage -r cache
```

Don’t go into `/private/var/folders` and delete things by hand. Besides this cache, that folder holds other apps’ temporary files and caches that are in use right now.

folders.name: Rust target folders
folders.question: Is it safe to delete a Rust project’s target folder?
folders.answer: **Yes.** `target` is everything Cargo compiled for the project, and none of it is source.
summary: **Yes.** `target` is everything Cargo compiled for the project, and none of it is source. `cargo clean` deletes it the official way.
**What it costs you:** the next build compiles the project and every dependency from scratch, a full build rather than a quick incremental one.
**Does it come back?** Yes, with the next `cargo build`, `cargo test` or editor check.
folders.comes_back: Yes, with the next `cargo build`, `cargo test` or editor check.
folders.what: Cargo writes all build output for a workspace into one `target` folder at the workspace root: compiled dependencies, your binaries and libraries, test executables, documentation, and incremental data that makes small rebuilds quick.
folders.how_to_clear:
From the project folder, with no build running:

```
cargo clean
```

With no options, that deletes the whole target directory. Narrower options:

- `cargo clean --release` removes only the `release` builds.
- `cargo clean --doc` removes only the generated docs.
- `cargo clean -p <crate>` cleans only that package.

folders.name: Safari’s cache and website data
folders.question: Is it safe to clear Safari’s cache and website data on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Yes.** The cache is copies of pages, images and scripts Safari saved so sites open faster, and Safari fetches them again as you browse.
summary: **Yes.** The cache is copies of pages, images and scripts Safari saved so sites open faster, and Safari fetches them again as you browse. Bookmarks, history and passwords are kept separately and stay.
**What it costs you:** slower first visits. Removing *website data* as well (cookies and site storage) signs you out of websites, and Apple notes it can change that data in other apps too.
**Does it come back?** Yes, the cache refills as you browse. Clear it from Safari’s own settings rather than by deleting folders.
folders.comes_back: Yes, the cache refills as you browse. Clear it from Safari’s own settings rather than by deleting folders.
folders.what: Safari keeps two kinds of things for the sites you visit. The **cache** is copies of page parts, such as images, scripts and style sheets, so a site you return to doesn’t download everything again. **Website data** is what sites store on purpose: cookies that keep you signed in, local storage, databases and offline data for web apps.
folders.how_to_clear:
### Cache, cookies and site data together

1. In Safari, choose **Safari › Settings**, then click **Privacy**.
2. Click **Manage Website Data**.
3. Select one or more websites and click **Remove**, or click **Remove All** to clear every site.

This is Apple’s own way to clear Safari’s cache and cookies. Removing sites one at a time keeps you signed in everywhere else.

### Only the cache

1. Choose **Safari › Settings**, click **Advanced** and turn on **Show features for web developers**. A Develop menu appears in the menu bar.
2. Choose **Develop › Empty Caches**.

Apple describes Empty Caches as emptying the webpage cache and Safari’s other caches. Cookies are a different kind of data, so this is the gentler choice when you only want stale pages gone.

**History › Clear History** is something else again: it removes the list of pages you visited, recent searches and similar records, and if Safari syncs through iCloud, Apple says it removes them from your other devices as well.

folders.name: Saved windows (Saved Application State)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete ~/Library/Saved Application State?
folders.answer: **Yes.** It only remembers which windows each app had open, and where, so they reappear when you reopen the app or restart the Mac.
summary: **Yes.** It only remembers which windows each app had open, and where, so they reappear when you reopen the app or restart the Mac. Your documents and settings aren’t in it.

**What it costs you:** the next time you open an app, it starts with a fresh window instead of your last layout. Save your work first: an app that brings back unsaved windows after a restart relies on it.
**Does it come back?** Yes. Apps write their saved state again as you use them, unless you turn the feature off.
folders.comes_back: Yes. Apps write their saved state again as you use them, unless you turn the feature off.
folders.what: macOS lets apps bring back their windows, tabs and positions when they reopen, after you quit them or after a restart. Each app saves that in a folder of its own here, named after its app ID with `.savedState` on the end, such as `com.apple.Preview.savedState`.
measure:
du -sh ~/Library/'Saved Application State'
du -sh ~/Library/'Saved Application State'/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -8
folders.how_to_clear:
For one app that misbehaves:

1. Quit the app.
2. Open `~/Library/Saved Application State` and move that app’s `.savedState` folder to the Trash.
3. Open the app again. It starts with a clean window.

For a fresh start without deleting anything, hold Shift while you open the app. Apple says the app then forgets the windows that were open when you last quit it, and no settings change.

To clear every app’s saved windows in Terminal, quit your apps first, then:

```
rm -rf ~/Library/'Saved Application State'/*
```

To stop windows coming back at all, turn on **Close windows when quitting an application** in System Settings › Desktop & Dock, and untick **Reopen windows when logging back in** in the dialog that appears when you shut down or restart.

folders.name: Slack’s cache
folders.question: Is it safe to clear Slack’s cache on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Yes.** Your messages, files and channels are kept in your Slack workspaces; the Mac app stores copies so it opens quickly.
summary: **Yes.** Your messages, files and channels are kept in your Slack workspaces; the Mac app stores copies so it opens quickly. Slack’s own **Help › Troubleshooting › Clear cache and restart** is the safe way to clear them.
**What it costs you:** a slower start while Slack loads your workspaces again. Emptying Slack’s whole data folder, which Slack suggests for update trouble, resets the app, so expect to sign in again.
**Does it come back?** Yes, as soon as Slack runs.
folders.comes_back: Yes, as soon as Slack runs.
folders.what: The Slack desktop app works much like a browser dedicated to Slack. It saves images, scripts and conversation data on your Mac so channels open without waiting. None of it is the only copy: messages and files you share are stored in your workspace, and Slack downloads what it needs again.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. In Slack, open the **Help** menu in the menu bar.
2. Choose **Troubleshooting**.
3. Click **Clear cache and restart**.

That’s enough for most people. Slack’s fix for update problems goes further: quit Slack, move the Slack app to the Trash, open the folder above for your version with **Go › Go to Folder** (⇧⌘G), move everything in it to the Trash and empty it, then download Slack again from slack.com.

In Terminal, the same reset for the slack.com version, with Slack quit:

```
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Slack/*
```

folders.name: The sleep image (sleepimage)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete /private/var/vm/sleepimage?
folders.answer: **No, leave it.** It’s where macOS saves a copy of memory so a sleeping Mac can pick up where it was, even if the battery runs out.
summary: **No, leave it.** It’s where macOS saves a copy of memory so a sleeping Mac can pick up where it was, even if the battery runs out. macOS writes it again the next time the Mac sleeps, so deleting it wins nothing for long.

**What losing it would cost:** protection for your open work if power fails while the Mac sleeps. The only real way to be rid of it is a power setting, and Apple’s documentation says to use caution with it.
**Does it come back?** Yes, by itself. On a laptop it’s part of normal sleep.
folders.comes_back: Yes, by itself. On a laptop it’s part of normal sleep.
folders.what: When a Mac sleeps, its memory stays powered so it can wake instantly. With *safe sleep*, macOS first writes a copy of memory to the disk, into this file. If power runs out while the Mac is asleep, it restores from that copy instead of losing everything that was open.
folders.how_to_clear:
Removing the file would take `sudo rm` on a system file, and it gains nothing: macOS writes a new one the next time the Mac sleeps. Don’t.

If you really want no sleep image, it’s the setting that matters, not the file. Apple’s `pmset` manual says hibernation images stop only when `hibernatemode`, `standby` and `autopoweroff` are all 0, and marks the hibernation settings “Please use caution”. On a laptop, that means a battery running flat during sleep takes your open work with it, so SiftMac’s advice is to keep the defaults.

To free space that stays free, look at what you control: [Time Machine’s local snapshots](https://siftmac.com/guides/time-machine-local-snapshots), [old macOS installers](https://siftmac.com/safe-to-delete/macos-installers) and the rest of [System Data](https://siftmac.com/guides/system-data-on-mac).

folders.name: Spotify’s cache and downloads
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Spotify’s cache on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Yes, the cache.** It’s parts of songs and podcasts Spotify saved so they play without stalling, and **Clear cache** in Spotify’s settings removes it safely.
summary: **Yes, the cache.** It’s parts of songs and podcasts Spotify saved so they play without stalling, and **Clear cache** in Spotify’s settings removes it safely. Playlists, likes and your library belong to your Spotify account, not to this Mac.
**What it costs you:** songs you play often stream again. **Downloads are different:** music saved for offline listening is gone until you download it again, online.
**Does it come back?** The cache does, as you listen. Downloads only come back if you download them again.
folders.comes_back: The cache does, as you listen. Downloads only come back if you download them again.
folders.what: Spotify’s help pages describe two separate uses of your storage: a **cache**, so music and podcasts play without lagging, and **downloads**, the albums, playlists and podcasts you saved to play offline. Downloading albums and playlists needs Premium; on the free plan you can download podcasts.
folders.how_to_clear:
### The cache

1. Open Spotify, click your profile picture at the top and choose **Settings**.
2. Scroll down to **Storage**.
3. Click **Clear cache**.

To keep the cache off a small startup disk, use **Change location** in the same section to store it somewhere else.

### Downloads

Spotify’s help says that when a computer runs short of space, you free it by removing downloaded tracks yourself, from the playlists, albums and podcasts you downloaded. Only remove what you’re happy to stream, or download again later with a connection.

Don’t delete `~/Library/Application Support/Spotify` to clear the cache: it’s Spotify’s data folder, so downloads and settings saved on this Mac would go with it.

folders.name: The Spotlight index (.Spotlight-V100)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete .Spotlight-V100 (the Spotlight index)?
folders.answer: **Not by hand.** `.Spotlight-V100` is one disk’s search index, the thing Spotlight, Finder’s search, Mail’s search and many apps look things up in.
summary: **Not by hand.** `.Spotlight-V100` is one disk’s search index, the thing Spotlight, Finder’s search, Mail’s search and many apps look things up in. If it’s huge or broken, have Spotlight rebuild it; on an external drive you never search, turn indexing off instead.
**What a rebuild costs you:** searches come up short for a while. Apple says indexing can take hours, or even days, depending on how much is on the disk.
**Does it come back?** Yes: Spotlight indexes the disk again, and the index grows back to fit what’s on it.
folders.comes_back: Yes: Spotlight indexes the disk again, and the index grows back to fit what’s on it.
folders.what: Spotlight reads your files and stores what it finds, names, text and details such as dates and authors, in an index, so a search answers at once instead of reading the whole disk. Every disk it indexes keeps its own index in a hidden folder at its top level, `.Spotlight-V100`.
folders.how_to_clear:
Apple’s way to rebuild the index of a disk or folder:

1. Open System Settings › Spotlight, or Siri & Spotlight on older versions of macOS.
2. Click Search Privacy, or Spotlight Privacy.
3. Add the disk or folder to the list, wait a few seconds, then select it and remove it again.
4. Click Done. Spotlight indexes it again from the start.

In Terminal, this erases the startup disk’s index so that Spotlight rebuilds it:

```
sudo mdutil -E /
```

For an external drive you never search, turn indexing off for it so the index doesn’t grow back, then remove the old one with Spotlight’s own tool rather than Finder (put the drive’s name in):

```
sudo mdutil -i off /Volumes/DriveName
sudo mdutil -X /Volumes/DriveName
```

To keep the index smaller, add folders you never search, such as virtual machines or build folders, to Search Privacy; Spotlight then leaves them out.

folders.name: Steam games and the Steam folder
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Steam games and the Steam folder on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Mostly.** A game you bought stays in your Steam library and can be installed again.
summary: **Mostly.** A game you bought stays in your Steam library and can be installed again. What you can lose is local save data for games that don’t use Steam Cloud, plus the time and data it takes to download the game again.
**What it costs you:** the download, and for some games their saves. Valve warns that if saves or other data are lost, Steam Support is unlikely to be able to recover them.
**Does it come back?** The game, yes, by installing it again. Saves only if they’re in Steam Cloud or you backed them up.
folders.comes_back: The game, yes, by installing it again. Saves only if they’re in Steam Cloud or you backed them up.
folders.what: Steam installs games inside its own folder in your Library, not in Applications. Valve’s instructions describe the `steamapps` folder (they write SteamApps) as holding your game downloads and any local save files. Next to it, `userdata` holds the local copies of Steam Cloud files: settings and saves for games that use the cloud.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Check the saves. Look for the Steam Cloud logo on the game’s store page, or in your Library right-click the game, choose **Properties…** and check **Cloud Synchronization** under General.
2. If the game doesn’t use Steam Cloud, back up its saves first; where they live varies, so check the game’s own help.
3. In your Steam Library, right-click the game and choose **Manage › Uninstall**.

### Removing Steam completely

Valve’s steps: quit Steam (**Steam › Quit Steam**), drag Steam from Applications to the Trash, then open `~/Library/Application Support/Steam`. To keep your games and saves, delete everything in it **except** `steamapps`; to remove everything, delete the whole Steam folder. Then empty the Trash.

If you remove it all and install Steam again later, Valve notes you’ll need your account name and password to download your games again.

folders.name: Swap files (swapfile)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete swap files (swapfile0, swapfile1…) on a Mac?
folders.answer: **No.** Swap files hold parts of memory macOS moved to the disk to make room.
summary: **No.** Swap files hold parts of memory macOS moved to the disk to make room. They’re in use for as long as your Mac runs, and macOS creates and removes them itself as memory demand changes.
**What to do instead:** close what’s using the memory. Quitting heavy apps brings swap use down, and after a restart the Mac starts with none in use.
**Does it come back?** Whenever memory runs short again. A lot of swap is a sign the Mac needs more memory for what you ask of it, not a cleaning problem.
folders.comes_back: Whenever memory runs short again. A lot of swap is a sign the Mac needs more memory for what you ask of it, not a cleaning problem.
folders.what: When memory runs short, macOS first compresses what it can’t spare. When that isn’t enough, it writes some of memory to the startup disk and reads it back when needed. Those pieces live in swap files named `swapfile0`, `swapfile1` and so on, and they’re encrypted.
folders.how_to_clear:
The files belong to the running system, and removing one would pull memory out from under running apps. macOS offers no way to delete them, and you don’t need one:

1. Open Activity Monitor, click Memory, and sort by the Memory column to see which apps use the most.
2. Quit what you don’t need: browsers with many tabs, virtual machines, large editors.
3. Restart if swap stays high. The Mac starts with fresh memory and nothing in swap.
4. If Memory Pressure is often yellow or red, the Mac could use more memory: Apple says yellow means it might eventually need more RAM, and red that it needs more. System Information shows whether yours can be upgraded; on Macs with Apple silicon it can’t, so it’s a choice for your next Mac.

folders.name: Swift Package Manager caches
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Swift Package Manager’s caches?
folders.answer: **Yes.** The shared cache in `~/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm` and each package’s `.build` folder are fetched or built again.
summary: **Yes.** The shared cache in `~/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm` and each package’s `.build` folder are fetched or built again. Keep `~/Library/org.swift.swiftpm`, which holds configuration and security records, not cache.
**What it costs you:** the next resolve fetches packages again, and the next build starts from scratch.
**Does it come back?** Yes, at the versions pinned in `Package.resolved`.
folders.comes_back: Yes, at the versions pinned in `Package.resolved`.
folders.what: Xcode projects that use Swift packages keep their checkouts and build products in the project’s DerivedData folder instead, which clears the way the [DerivedData guide](https://siftmac.com/guides/xcode-deriveddata) describes.

| Command | What it removes |
| --- | --- |
| `swift package clean` | Build artifacts in `.build`; dependency checkouts stay |
| `swift package reset` | The package’s complete cache and build directory |
| `swift package purge-cache` | The global repository cache shared by all packages |

```
cd ~/Projects/MyPackage

```

In Xcode, the File › Packages menu has Reset Package Caches and Resolve Package Versions for the open project.

folders.name: System-wide caches (/Library/Caches)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete /Library/Caches on a Mac?
folders.answer: **No, leave it to macOS.**
summary: **No, leave it to macOS.** This is the cache folder shared by every account on the Mac and by background services, and much of it belongs to macOS itself. Parts of it are guarded, so you couldn’t clear everything even if you tried.

**What clearing it by hand costs:** an administrator password, for little space. The supported reset for system caches is a safe-mode startup, which clears some of them and lets macOS make them again.
**Does it come back?** Yes. Whatever is cleared is rebuilt as it’s needed, which is the other reason clearing it rarely pays.
folders.comes_back: Yes. Whatever is cleared is rebuilt as it’s needed, which is the other reason clearing it rarely pays.
folders.what: `/Library/Caches`, at the top level of the startup disk rather than in your home folder, is the cache folder for the whole Mac. macOS services keep caches here that serve every account, such as icon and color data, and apps that install parts for all users, like updaters, drivers and background helpers, can keep theirs here too.
folders.how_to_clear:
For macOS’s own caches, use Apple’s way: start up in safe mode once, then restart normally. Apple’s support article says safe mode clears some system caches, including font caches and the kernel cache, which are created again automatically as needed.

1. On a Mac with Apple silicon: shut down, then press and hold the power button until the startup options appear. Select your startup disk, hold Shift and click Continue in Safe Mode.
2. On an Intel Mac: turn it on or restart, and hold Shift until the login window appears.
3. Log in. “Safe Boot” shows in the menu bar of the login window. Then restart normally.

For a third-party app’s folder that has grown large, use the app’s own settings or uninstaller first. If the app is already gone, move its folder from `/Library/Caches` to the Trash in Finder and enter your administrator password when asked. Leave Apple’s folders alone, and don’t use `sudo rm` here.

folders.answer: **Yes.** Telegram stores your chats and media in its cloud, and what’s on your Mac is a cache.
summary: **Yes.** Telegram stores your chats and media in its cloud, and what’s on your Mac is a cache. Telegram’s FAQ points to **Clear cache** in its storage settings as the way to free space without logging out.

**Does it come back?** Yes. Telegram says media removed from the cache stays in the cloud and downloads again the moment you open it.
folders.comes_back: Yes. Telegram says media removed from the cache stays in the cloud and downloads again the moment you open it.
folders.what: Telegram’s chats, photos, videos and files live on its servers. Each device keeps a local cache of what you’ve opened, so it shows again without a download. Telegram’s FAQ says that with its cloud and cache settings it can take up nearly zero space on a device.

folders.name: The Trash
folders.question: Is it safe to empty the Trash on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Yes, once you’ve looked through it.**
summary: **Yes, once you’ve looked through it.** Everything in the Trash is something you already chose to delete, and emptying it is what actually gives the space back.
**What it costs you:** your last easy way back. Until then, File › Put Back returns an item to where it was; afterwards, Apple says, emptied items are permanently deleted.
**Does it come back?** No. Only a backup made before can bring an emptied item back. The Trash itself fills up again as you delete things.
folders.comes_back: No. Only a backup made before can bring an emptied item back. The Trash itself fills up again as you delete things.
folders.what: Moving a file to the Trash doesn’t delete it. Apple’s guide is plain about it: items aren’t deleted until you empty the Trash. Until then they take exactly as much space as before, which is why throwing away a large video doesn’t change your free space.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Open the Trash from the Dock, switch to list view and click the Size column to see the biggest items.
2. Drag out anything you want to keep, or select it and choose File › Put Back.
3. Connect any external drive you deleted files from, so its Trash empties too.
4. Click **Empty** in the top-right corner of the window, then Empty Trash.

To delete just one item for good and keep the rest, Control-click it and choose Delete Immediately.

To have macOS empty it for you, choose Finder › Settings › Advanced and select “Remove items from the Trash after 30 days”; Storage settings offers the same as Empty Trash Automatically. Items you delete from iCloud Drive leave the Trash after 30 days whatever you choose.

folders.name: UTM virtual machines (.utm)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete UTM virtual machines (.utm)?
folders.answer: **Yes, when you no longer need the guest.**
summary: **Yes, when you no longer need the guest.** Each VM is a `.utm` package that holds its drives, so deleting it deletes the guest system and every file in it. Do it from UTM: its Remove action also deletes the data of VMs stored in UTM’s default place.
**What it costs you:** the whole guest, with no undo. Installer ISOs attached as removable drives aren’t inside the package, so they stay.
**Does it come back?** No. Export or clone a VM first if you might want it later.
folders.comes_back: No. Export or clone a VM first if you might want it later.
folders.what: UTM runs virtual machines on a Mac with either Apple’s virtualization backend or QEMU. Each VM is a `.utm` package: Finder shows one file, but inside are the VM’s configuration and its drives.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Shut the VM down and copy out any files you want from inside it.
2. In UTM, secondary-click the VM in the list to open its action menu.
3. Choose Remove. If the VM is stored in UTM’s default place and hasn’t been moved, its data is deleted too. A VM stored elsewhere is only taken off the list, and its `.utm` package stays where it is.

From Terminal, UTM’s `utmctl` tool deletes a VM by name or UUID, and UTM’s documentation notes there’s no confirmation:

```
/Applications/UTM.app/Contents/MacOS/utmctl list
/Applications/UTM.app/Contents/MacOS/utmctl delete "<VM name>"
```

**To keep a VM but use less space**, delete snapshots you don’t need in its Snapshots tab, and discard a suspended state you don’t need with Delete under Current State. Then, for QEMU drives, the drive’s settings offer Reclaim Space and Compress, which rewrite the image without the zeroed space. UTM calls both experimental, says to back up the VM first, converts raw images to QCOW2 when you use them, and can’t reclaim space while snapshots or a suspended state exist.

Running TRIM inside the guest first, such as `fstrim` on Linux, and then shutting the VM down, lets Reclaim Space free more.

folders.name: uv’s cache (~/.cache/uv)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete uv’s cache?
folders.answer: **Yes, with uv’s commands.**
summary: **Yes, with uv’s commands.** uv’s docs call the cache disposable, but say never to remove files or folders inside it by hand. `uv cache prune` and `uv cache clean` are the way.
**What it costs you:** the next `uv sync` or `uv pip install` downloads and builds again, so it’s slower and needs the network.
**Does it come back?** Yes, as soon as uv installs anything.
folders.comes_back: Yes, as soon as uv installs anything.
folders.what: uv caches answers from package indexes, downloaded wheels and source distributions, wheels it built itself, and the unpacked files it installs from. Installing into an environment then comes down to placing files from the cache, which keeps repeat installs fast.
folders.how_to_clear:
Two commands, from gentle to complete:

- `uv cache prune` removes unused entries, such as ones left by earlier uv versions, and the centralized project environments uv keeps there, which it recreates when needed. uv’s docs say it’s safe to run periodically.
- `uv cache clean` removes every entry. `uv cache clean <package>`, for example `uv cache clean ruff`, removes only that package’s entries.

```
uv cache prune
uv cache clean
```

Run them while no other uv command is working. uv locks the cache while it changes it and waits up to five minutes for other uv processes; `--force` skips that wait, and is only safe when nothing else is using the cache.
clear_commands:
uv cache prune
uv cache clean

folders.name: Temporary files (/private/var/folders)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete /private/var/folders on a Mac?
folders.answer: **No, not by hand.**
summary: **No, not by hand.** It holds every account’s temporary folder and a second cache folder, both in use right now by running apps and macOS services. Deleting from it underneath them can make them fail until you restart.

**What to do instead:** let macOS clear it. Apple documents that temporary files untouched for three days may be removed by the system, and that the cache folder is emptied when the Mac starts up in safe mode.
**Does it come back?** All the time: everything that runs uses it, so it’s never empty, and isn’t meant to be.
folders.comes_back: All the time: everything that runs uses it, so it’s never empty, and isn’t meant to be.
folders.what: Each account on the Mac gets a private set of folders under `/private/var/folders`, at a path that looks random, such as `/private/var/folders/xy/a1b2c3…/`. Inside are three folders:
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Restart. Apps that were running let go of their temporary files, and macOS’s cleanup runs as the Mac starts up.
2. If one app’s folder in `T` or `C` is huge, quit that app, then move just that folder, or those files, to the Trash. The name usually says which app it is.
3. To empty the cache folder, start up in safe mode once, then restart normally.

Never run `rm -rf` on `/private/var/folders`, with or without `sudo`. It deletes files that background services have open, along with other accounts’ files.

folders.name: VirtualBox virtual machines
folders.question: Is it safe to delete the VirtualBox VMs folder?
folders.answer: **Yes, VM by VM, from VirtualBox.**
summary: **Yes, VM by VM, from VirtualBox.** Each folder in `~/VirtualBox VMs` is one virtual machine: its settings file, its virtual disks and its snapshots. Removing a VM with its files deletes the guest system and everything saved in it.
**What it costs you:** the whole guest. Deleting folders in Finder instead leaves VirtualBox listing a machine whose files are gone, so remove VMs in VirtualBox Manager or with `VBoxManage`.
**Does it come back?** No. Copy or export a VM first if you might need it again.
folders.comes_back: No. Copy or export a VM first if you might need it again.
folders.what: VirtualBox gives every virtual machine a folder of its own, which Oracle’s manual calls the VM folder. By default they all sit together in a folder called `VirtualBox VMs` in your home folder. A VM folder holds:
measure:
du -sh ~/VirtualBox\ VMs/* | sort -h
VBoxManage list vms
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Shut the VM down: VirtualBox disables Remove while a VM is running.
2. In VirtualBox Manager, click Machines, then Control-click the VM in the machine list and choose Remove.
3. In the dialog, choose to remove the VM’s files as well, not just its entry in the list.

From Terminal, `VBoxManage` does the same in one step:

```
VBoxManage unregistervm "<VM name>" --delete
```

With `--delete`, VirtualBox deletes the VM’s hard disk images, differencing images included, its saved state files, one for each snapshot, its settings file and backups, its logs, and its folder once it’s empty. `--delete-all` also deletes DVD and floppy images in the VM’s folder that are attached only to this VM.

**To keep a VM but shrink its disk**, first delete snapshots you no longer need in the VM’s Snapshots tab; Oracle notes this can take a long time and needs temporary disk space while it runs. Then zero out the free space inside the guest, shut the VM down and compact the disk:

```
VBoxManage modifymedium disk "<path to disk>.vdi" --compact
```

Compacting removes blocks that contain only zeroes, so it only frees what the guest has zeroed, with tools Oracle names such as `sdelete -z` in Windows or `zerofree` for Linux ext2 and ext3 file systems. It works on VDI images only.

folders.name: VS Code’s caches and extensions
folders.question: Is it safe to delete VS Code’s caches and old extensions?
folders.answer: **Yes, the caches**, with VS Code quit.
summary: **Yes, the caches**, with VS Code quit. Folders like `Cache`, `CachedData` and `GPUCache` in `~/Library/Application Support/Code` hold files VS Code makes again. Old versions of extensions can go too, but remove extensions you don’t use from inside VS Code.
**What it costs you:** a slightly slower first start while VS Code rebuilds its caches. Your settings, extensions and workspaces stay as they are.
**Does it come back?** Yes. The caches refill as you work, and each extension update adds a new version folder.
folders.comes_back: Yes. The caches refill as you work, and each extension update adds a new version folder.
folders.what: Visual Studio Code is built on Electron, so like a browser it keeps caches to start and draw faster. They live in its user data folder, `~/Library/Application Support/Code`, next to things that aren’t caches at all:
folders.how_to_clear:
**Caches.** Quit VS Code (`⌘Q`), then clear the cache folders and leave `User` and everything else alone:

```
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/Cache/*
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/"Code Cache"/*
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/GPUCache/*
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/CachedData/*
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/CachedExtensionVSIXs/*
```

**Extensions you don’t use.** Uninstall them in VS Code: open the Extensions view (`⇧⌘X`), click the gear on the extension and choose Uninstall. Or from Terminal, with the `code` command:

```
code --list-extensions --show-versions
code --uninstall-extension <publisher.name>
```

**Old versions of an extension.** `--show-versions` prints the version of each extension VS Code has installed. A folder in `~/.vscode/extensions` for the same extension with a different version is a copy it no longer uses, and can go to the Trash with VS Code quit. If you use profiles, list each one too (`code --list-extensions --show-versions --profile <name>`) before deleting anything.

rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/Cache/*
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/"Code Cache"/*
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/GPUCache/*
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/CachedData/*
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/Code/CachedExtensionVSIXs/*

folders.name: WhatsApp’s media and data
folders.question: Is it safe to delete WhatsApp’s media and data on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Be careful.** WhatsApp for Mac holds a copy of your recent chats and the photos, videos and files in them.
summary: **Be careful.** WhatsApp for Mac holds a copy of your recent chats and the photos, videos and files in them. Most of it is also on your phone, but not necessarily all of it: anything your phone no longer has may exist only here.
**What it costs you:** WhatsApp says that deleting a message, for yourself or for everyone, syncs to all your devices that are online. Delete media inside the Mac app and it goes from your phone too.
**Does it come back?** Only what your phone still has. When you link a Mac, your phone sends it your recent history.
folders.comes_back: Only what your phone still has. When you link a Mac, your phone sends it your recent history.
folders.what: WhatsApp for Mac is a linked device. WhatsApp’s help explains that right after you link it, your phone sends an end-to-end encrypted copy of your most recent message history, which is then stored locally on the Mac. Not every chat or message is copied over; WhatsApp says the Mac app can show up to three years of history, and to check your phone for the full record.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. **Save what you want to keep.** Open the photos, videos and documents that matter and save them to a folder you keep, or to Photos. Check that your phone still has the chats you care about.
2. **Remember that deletes sync.** Deleting a message in the Mac app removes it on your other devices too, so only do it for things you want gone everywhere.
3. **To stop using WhatsApp on this Mac,** log out: open WhatsApp’s **Settings**, choose **Log out**, and confirm. Your phone keeps its chats. WhatsApp doesn’t say what logging out does to the Mac’s local copy, so measure the folder again afterwards.

Don’t delete the folder by hand to save space. It’s WhatsApp’s database, not just its media, WhatsApp doesn’t document deleting it, and you’d have to link the Mac again to use the app.

folders.name: Xcode Archives
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Xcode’s Archives folder?
folders.answer: **Partly.** Archives of builds nobody runs any more can go.
summary: **Partly.** Archives of builds nobody runs any more can go. Keep the archive of every version people still use: Apple says to retain the archive of each build you distribute, because its debug symbols (dSYMs) are what make that version’s crash reports readable.

**What it costs you:** for each archive you delete, the ability to add symbol names to that build’s crash reports on this Mac, and to export or upload that exact build again. Your source code isn’t in it.
**Does it come back?** No. Archiving the same code again makes a new build with a different build UUID, and a dSYM only works with the binary it was made with.
folders.comes_back: No. Archiving the same code again makes a new build with a different build UUID, and a dSYM only works with the binary it was made with.
folders.what: When you choose Product › Archive, Xcode builds your app for release and saves the result as an archive, a `.xcarchive` bundle that appears in the Archives organizer (Window › Organizer). From there you validate it, upload it to App Store Connect for TestFlight or the App Store, or export it to distribute some other way.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Decide which versions still matter: anything people still run from the App Store or TestFlight, and builds you sent to customers or testers directly. Keep those archives.
2. In Xcode, choose Window › Organizer and click Archives. Pick an app in the sidebar to see its archives with version and build numbers.
3. Select the archives of versions nobody uses any more and delete them. Or, with Xcode quit, move whole dated folders from `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/Archives` to the Trash in Finder and empty it.

If you might still look at crashes from a build but want the space, keep just its symbols: open the archive’s package contents and copy the `dSYMs` folder somewhere you’ll keep, named by version and build. When Xcode can’t symbolicate an address, Apple suggests finding the matching dSYM with Spotlight, so keep the copy in a folder Spotlight indexes.

> If you uploaded symbols with a build to App Store Connect, the crash reports Apple delivers to Xcode’s Crashes organizer already carry symbol names. A crash-reporting service you use may still need the dSYMs, so check it has them before deleting the archive.

folders.name: Xcode simulators (CoreSimulator)
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Xcode simulators and CoreSimulator?
folders.answer: **Yes, with Xcode’s own tools.**
summary: **Yes, with Xcode’s own tools.** Simulators for OS versions you’ve removed are dead weight, and ones you don’t use can go too. Delete them with Xcode or `xcrun simctl`, not in Finder, so CoreSimulator’s list of devices stays right.
**What it costs you:** the test apps and data on each simulator you delete. Simulator runtimes, the simulated OS versions, download again from Xcode if you need one back.
**Does it come back?** A simulator is added again in Xcode in moments, empty. A runtime comes back from Xcode › Settings › Components.
folders.comes_back: A simulator is added again in Xcode in moments, empty. A runtime comes back from Xcode › Settings › Components.
folders.what: A simulator is a simulated iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch or other Apple device, tied to one OS version. CoreSimulator keeps each one as a folder named by its UDID, holding everything on it: the builds you installed, their data and documents, and the device’s settings.
measure:
du -sh ~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/* ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/UserData/Previews 2>/dev/null
xcrun simctl list devices
xcrun simctl runtime list
folders.how_to_clear:
**Simulators for OS versions you’ve removed.** They can’t run any more, so they can all go at once. Quit Simulator, then:

```
xcrun simctl delete unavailable
```

**Simulators you don’t use.** Take the UDID from `xcrun simctl list devices` and delete just that one:

```
xcrun simctl delete <UDID>
```

**Runtimes you no longer target.** In Xcode, choose Xcode › Settings, click Components, click the info button next to the runtime and choose Delete. Apple’s support staff describe this as the intended way. From Terminal:

```
xcrun simctl runtime list
xcrun simctl runtime delete <runtime-id>
```

**SwiftUI preview simulators.** With Xcode quit, `xcrun simctl --set previews delete all` clears the preview device set; developers on Apple’s forums report previews working normally afterwards.

> Avoid deleting folders inside `Devices` by hand. CoreSimulator keeps its own record of the devices it manages, and `simctl` removes the record and the folder together.
clear_commands:
xcrun simctl runtime list
xcrun simctl runtime delete <runtime-id>

folders.name: Yarn’s cache
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Yarn’s cache?
folders.answer: **Yes**, with one exception.
summary: **Yes**, with one exception. The global caches hold packages Yarn already downloaded. A project’s own `.yarn/cache` folder may be committed to Git on purpose, so check before deleting that one.
**What it costs you:** the next `yarn install` downloads again, and Yarn 2+ projects using Plug’n’Play can’t run until it has.
**Does it come back?** Yes, with every install.
folders.comes_back: Yes, with every install.
folders.what: Yarn comes in two lines that store packages differently. Run `yarn --version` inside a project to see which one it uses: 1.x is Yarn Classic, and anything from 2 up is modern Yarn, often called Berry.
folders.how_to_clear:
Use the Yarn that owns the cache:

- **Yarn Classic:** `yarn cache clean` clears the global cache. Name packages to clear only those, for example `yarn cache clean left-pad`.
- **Yarn 2+:** inside a project, `yarn cache clean --mirror` removes the global cache files in `~/.yarn`, plain `yarn cache clean` removes that project’s local cache files, and `yarn cache clean --all` removes both.

```
yarn cache clean            # Yarn 1: the global cache
yarn cache clean --mirror   # Yarn 2+: the global cache
```

Before clearing a project’s `.yarn/cache`, run `git status` there or look in `.gitignore`. If Git tracks the folder, it’s part of the project rather than a leftover, and deleting it shows up as a long list of deleted files.
clear_commands:
yarn cache clean            # Yarn 1: the global cache
yarn cache clean --mirror   # Yarn 2+: the global cache

folders.name: Zoom recordings and cache
folders.question: Is it safe to delete Zoom recordings and Zoom’s cache on a Mac?
folders.answer: **Your call.** A computer recording is a video Zoom made on this Mac, and it may be the only copy: Zoom’s help notes it can only be played on the device where it was made.
summary: **Your call.** A computer recording is a video Zoom made on this Mac, and it may be the only copy: Zoom’s help notes it can only be played on the device where it was made. Once deleted and out of the Trash, it’s gone.
**What it costs you:** the meeting’s video and audio, unless you copied them somewhere else. Cloud recordings, if you use them, live in your Zoom account and aren’t affected.
**Does it come back?** No. Zoom’s cache is a different matter: Zoom’s own help has you move its `data` folder to the Trash.
folders.comes_back: No. Zoom’s cache is a different matter: Zoom’s own help has you move its `data` folder to the Trash.
folders.what: When you record a meeting to your computer, Zoom writes a folder for that meeting in your Documents folder, then converts it into ordinary video and audio files after the meeting ends. These are your files, like any video you shot. Zoom can’t make them again.
folders.how_to_clear:
1. Decide what you need. Play the start of anything you’re unsure about, and copy keepers to another drive or a cloud folder first.
2. In the Zoom app, go to the **Home** tab and click **Open recordings**, then **My files › Meeting recordings › Computer recordings**.
3. Hover over a recording, click the **…** button, choose **Delete** and confirm.

You can also move meeting folders from `~/Documents/Zoom` to the Trash in Finder, and empty it once you’re sure. Deleting a recording in Zoom’s web portal only takes it off the list there; the files stay on your Mac.

### Zoom’s cache and cookies

Zoom’s own steps: in Finder choose **Go › Go to Folder**, open `~/Library/Application Support/zoom.us` and move the **data** folder to the Trash. Quit Zoom first.
